WebAssembly Components vs Containers: Two Ways to Package a Program

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A service can be shipped as a container image that includes a base operating system, libraries and the application, or as a WebAssembly component that contains only compiled code and a description of the functions it imports and exports.
  • A container bundles a filesystem and process tree so almost any program runs unchanged, while a WebAssembly component bundles code with a typed interface and a capability boundary, starting in milliseconds and carrying far less baggage — at the price of a restricted execution model.
  • The container won because it made legacy applications trivial to move.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A service can be shipped as a container image that includes a base operating system, libraries and the application, or as a WebAssembly component that contains only compiled code and a description of the functions it imports and exports. Both deploy the same logic to a server, and both are portable. They differ in what they assume about the world around them and in how much trust a platform must extend to them.

A container bundles a filesystem and process tree so almost any program runs unchanged, while a WebAssembly component bundles code with a typed interface and a capability boundary, starting in milliseconds and carrying far less baggage — at the price of a restricted execution model.

The container won because it made legacy applications trivial to move. The component model is interesting because it makes a different bet: that many services do not need a whole operating system and benefit from being sandboxed by default.

The container is a packaging trick around Linux namespaces and cgroups. It gives a process an isolated view of the filesystem, network and process table, and an image layers the files it needs on top of a base. This is why a program written decades ago can run in a modern cluster with little change. The cost is size and startup time: an image is often hundreds of megabytes, and booting a container means mounting layers and starting a full process with a complete user-space environment.

Sources indicate that A WebAssembly component starts from a different place. The module is compiled to a small binary format with no built-in access to files, network or system calls; it receives capabilities explicitly from its host. The component model adds typed imports and exports, so a module can declare that it needs a key-value store or an HTTP client and let the host supply it. A component is usually kilobytes to a few megabytes and can start in single-digit milliseconds.

A container image is typically tens to hundreds of megabytes and starts in hundreds of milliseconds, while a WebAssembly component is often under a few megabytes and starts in under ten milliseconds because there is no guest kernel to boot — but it can only call capabilities the host provides.

The mechanism is the boundary between the program and the host. A container isolates by reusing the host kernel and hiding parts of the system from the process, which is strong but not airtight; a kernel bug or a privileged container can escape. WebAssembly has no system calls at all, so a module cannot open a file unless the host hands it a handle, and the interface between the two is defined by types rather than conventions.

That restriction is also the friction. Anything a component needs must be expressed as an import the host understands, and the ecosystem of interfaces is still growing. Plugins written for a container world expect environment variables, sockets and files, and porting them to components means redesigning how they receive dependencies. The sandbox that makes components safe is the same thing that makes existing code need work.

It has been revealed that the everyday analogy is a phone app versus a program you install on a laptop. The laptop program can reach anywhere the operating system lets it, which is flexible and occasionally dangerous; the phone app must ask for each permission, which is safer and sometimes frustrating. Components are the phone-app model for servers, and that indicates up when a plugin from an untrusted source runs next to your own code without being able to read its memory.

Edge computing is where the difference becomes concrete. A function that must start on demand across thousands of small locations benefits from a tiny, fast-starting artifact more than from a full container, especially when the platform wants to pack many tenants onto one machine. A long-running monolithic service with a complex runtime still fits a container better.

Choose containers when you need to run existing software with minimal changes; choose WebAssembly components when you control the code, want millisecond cold starts and a hard capability boundary, and can express dependencies as typed interfaces.

These two are converging in places, with container runtimes gaining WebAssembly support, but the underlying bets remain different. One abstracts the machine so anything can run; the other defines a small contract so only safe things can run.

According to recent reports, for a team deciding today, the question is not which technology wins but how much of the stack you control. Control the code and the deployment target, and components buy real safety and speed. Inherit a pile of existing services, and containers remain the pragmatic choice.

In a recent development, the container and serverless runtime market is valued in the tens of billions of dollars annually, and a meaningful slice of fresh function-as-a-service deployments now uses WebAssembly for cold-start-sensitive workloads. If even a modest share of edge and plugin workloads moves to components, the tooling and runtime ecosystem around it becomes a multi-billion-dollar layer rather than a curiosity.

These are order-of-magnitude estimates from published market ranges and stated assumptions, not a forecast for any vendor.

Containers package an operating system and run anything; WebAssembly components package a small capability-limited module that starts in milliseconds and travels with a precise interface.

#46431. Industry News: AI Customer Service Hallucination: Real Examples and Fixes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (742 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AI Customer Service Hallucination: Real Examples and Fixes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hallucination in customer service is not an abstract model problem.
  • In a recent development, A ticket had 25 back-and-forth messages.
  • Fix: no model receives a raw thread any more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hallucination in customer service is not an abstract model problem. It is a reply that promises a refund nobody approved, quotes a policy that does not exist, or tells a customer to send a video they already sent. Below are six we caught in a production system that answers customer email and chat for an e-bike brand in eight languages, what caused each one, and the change that stopped it. In almost every case the cause was the input, not the model.

In a recent development, A ticket had 25 back-and-forth messages. Somewhere in the middle, the team had promised a full refund once the return reached the warehouse. The model writing the next reply did not see it and wrote something that contradicted the promise. A stronger model given the same thread got it right, which told us what was missing: the model had all the material and could not find what mattered in it.

Fix: no model receives a raw thread any more. Code and a dedicated extraction step turn the history into a short list of facts, each with source and date: what the customer wants now, what we promised, what has been done, what the customer has already sent, what is missing, and what conflicts. On one order this cut the input from 37,604 tokens to 4,722 and every item in the reply came out right.

On a content pipeline, the prompt noted "always name the place in Chinese and English", "always give a number when you mention a cost" and "never invent a business name". When the source had no shop names or prices, the first two rules forced the model to write something and the third forbade it. The model picked the first two and invented names.

Fix: rewrite the forcing rules to "write it when the material has it; otherwise leave it out". The invented names disappeared. The general lesson: when a model invents, look for a rule that demands output the material cannot supply.

A customer asked whether a promotion still applied. The AI answered wrongly. When we asked ourselves how we knew it was wrong, the answer was simple: we knew today's date and the model did not. Giving the model the current date fixed it without a single fresh rule.

Fix: after every mistake, write down the fact you used to spot it, then make sure the model receives that fact. This beats adding "be careful about promotions" to the prompt.

A customer included a police report reference in their email. The order-number extractor matched the first part of it as an order number and linked the ticket to another customer's order. The AI then answered with someone else's shipping status.

In a recent development, fix: tighten the pattern, then scan production emails for every string with the same shape before shipping the fresh pattern. The same scan found a second problem: a full-width colon used in Chinese text made one extractor drop an entire email. Extractors now accept both full-width and half-width punctuation.

According to recent reports, in a review of 400 drafts that agents edited before sending, 10% of the edits replaced "we do not have this information" with an answer the knowledge base already contained. The model was not lying about the world; it had not been shown the right entry.

In a recent development, fix: the system now searches the knowledge base before every draft, one short query per question in the email, and passes the hits to the model. Retrieval quality depended mostly on the query: a short, single-topic question put the right FAQ entry first.

Industry observers note that when a customer replied to an older thread, an automatic send went out with a draft written for the previous message. The reply was fluent and wrong for the upcoming email.

According to recent reports, fix: anything sent automatically is generated fresh for the email it answers. Earlier drafts and earlier cases can inform the judgement; they are never sent as they are.

The same system and its numbers are in our customer service case study. For the wider pattern of agents breaking in production, see why AI agents fail in production. If you want this applied to your own support desk, the free plan maps it to your work in two working days.

It has been revealed that the perfect burger can be hard to come by. When you're going out, Food Republic's list of the best burgers in every state can be helpful, and there are even some great fast food options. But when you're looking for a super juicy and flavorful homemade grilled or pan-fried patty, what's the best route to take?

According to recent reports, sometimes, it all comes down to what you mix into the ground beef. While Bobby Flay uses only salt and pepper to season his patties, some folks swear by Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder for a kick of flavor. But there's one ingredient you may not have thought of that will keep your end result wonderfully succulent. Try mixing some onion dip into your ground beef. It's one of the clever ingredients that make burgers juicier, and it will add loads of flavor.

Recent findings suggest that onion dips generally come seasoned with dried onion and garlic, salt, and other herbs, plus a little sugar for sweetness. Add to that the sour cream base, and you have a rich, bold, slightly tangy, umami-filled burst of flavor that won't overpower your taste buds. And because you're mixing the dip directly into the beef before cooking, it can help keep your patties nice and moist (as long as you don't overcook them). Sour cream is simply cultured cream, so it has a high moisture content, and the added seasonings aren't so coarse that they will burn before the beef itself is cooked.

When it comes to what dip to use, classics like Dean's French Onion or Daisy Sour Cream French Onion, which is available on Amazon, will work great, but pretty much any brand will work. Depending on how much tangy flavor you want, you'll need about a half-cup to a full cup of dip per 2 pounds of beef.

The beauty of using onion dip in your burgers is that it's a one-ingredient solution, but you can increase the intensity with extra onion powder or fresh minced or dried onions. Just don't overdo it on the onion pieces, or the patties could fall apart on the grill. If you're going heavy on the amount of dip you use, you may want to think about adding some breadcrumbs as a binding agent. Dried parsley makes a great mix-in, as do other Italian herbs, but you should start sparingly so they don't overpower the flavor you're aiming for.

Industry observers note that as for toppings, the regular stuff will do, but you might want to hold off on the ketchup and mustard until you've had a bite. Caramelized onions are an obvious choice, or you can give your burger some crunch with crispy fried onions. And you can always add an extra dollop of onion dip on top for more creamy flavor and texture.

Lastly, this trick will also work with a dried dip mix. Just mix it in with sour cream before you make the burgers. And if you want a similarly juicy bite without the added zing, try using mayonnaise in your burger. But for a juicy texture and plenty of zesty flavor, grab that onion dip out of the fridge.

Who Makes Costco's Kirkland Signature Red Blend Wine?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (428 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola.
  • In a recent development, A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend.
  • DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola. Yet one unknown that perpetually probes consumers is which producer is behind Costco's private-label alcohol. The Kirkland Signature labels conceal a treasure trove of well-priced bottles, spanning not only every major liquor style, but also a varied selection of wine and (formerly) beer.

In a recent development, A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend. This vino comes packaged in an eye-catching 1.5-liter bottle, all while sold for under $10. You'd think that such a size would make sleuthing the producer tricky. However, the brand behind this budget pick is listed directly on the bottle: DC Flynt MW Selections. A large manufacturer responsible for both cellaring and bottling, this producer and distributor oversees a widespread U.S. and global portfolio, making it a natural match for Costco.

DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California. This suggests that at least some of the grapes are assembled in California's Central Valley region, as Modesto is only about two hours from Napa Valley — although precise vineyard sourcing is unknown. The same brand is also behind bottles from Sonoma, Napa, and Alexander Valley. Similarly, it produces Kirkland Signature's chardonnay as well.

As one of the least expensive Kirkland Signature wines, you might not expect an oenophile-appreciated experience with this bottle. Yet despite this accessible price point, the wine garners positive reviews: "A proof that [mass-marketed] wines can actually be good," noted Vivino reviewer Anton A., who gave the wine 4 stars. On the platform, the wine is rated 3.7 out of 5 stars, with over 3,500 reviews. Furthermore, other reviewers have given it favorable scores, praising the wine's balance of fruit-forward and spice flavors.

Recent findings suggest that typically, affordable California red blends are known for sweet "jammy" flavors, meaning the composition is heavy on sugar. Yet as noted right on the Kirkland label itself, this bottling strays from aggressive fruit-forwardness. Notes of oak and spice help contrast the fruit, a sentiment upheld by reviewers: "More [Bordeaux-like] than a California fruit bomb, but extremely tasty," noted another Vivino user — although some drinkers do take matter with its moderate palate. #46422. Agentic AI vs Generative AI: The Difference at Work

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (621 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Agentic AI vs Generative AI: The Difference at Work

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Generative AI produces content when you ask for it.
  • The clearest way to see the difference is to give both the same piece of work.
  • Industry observers note that A customer writes: "Where is my order?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Generative AI produces content when you ask for it. Agentic AI uses the same kind of model to carry out a task: it decides what it needs, looks it up, and acts. The first answers a prompt. The second finishes a job.

The clearest way to see the difference is to give both the same piece of work.

Industry observers note that A customer writes: "Where is my order? It has been ten days.".

Generative AI. You paste the email into a model and ask for a reply. It writes a polite, well-formed message: an apology for the wait and a promise to look into it. It contains no tracking status, because the model has none. The customer learns nothing, and someone still has to look the order up.

Agentic AI. The system reads the email, finds the order, asks the carrier for the status, checks the delivery time the store's policy states, and writes a reply that gives the latest tracking event with its date and place. If tracking shows a real problem, it also creates the task for a person to contact the carrier.

It has been revealed that same model family, same email. The second version did the work the first one only talked about.

This is why a generative tool is running in an afternoon and an agentic system takes a project. The connection work is described in connecting orders and shipping.

Generative AI gets words wrong. It states a fact that is false, or writes in the wrong tone. A person reading the output catches it.

According to recent reports, agentic AI gets actions wrong. It tells a customer an address was changed when nobody changed it. It records an amount that a person later altered. It sends a reply built on a lookup that failed. Nobody reads these in advance if the system acts alone.

In a recent development, so the controls differ. Generative output needs review of the text. Agentic work needs:.

Recent findings suggest that A generative request is one call to a model. An agentic task is several: decide, call a tool, read the result, decide again, write. The cost per task is higher and so is the time. In the deployment we run, the replies the AI sends alone go out a median of 6.3 minutes after the customer's email, counted on 19 November 2026.

A production system is not one or the other. In the email flow we operate, the path is fixed: gather the facts, decide the solution, write the reply, check it. Inside the "gather" and "decide" steps, the model is free to choose which tools to call. The writing step is plain generation from the facts the earlier steps produced. The design is described in AI agent vs workflow.

Keeping generation and action apart has a practical benefit: when a reply is wrong, you can tell whether the facts were wrong or the wording was.

Sources indicate that customer service is the second kind. In 30 days to 19 November 2026, the system we run received 36,789 customer emails and 15,725 chat conversations. Answering them means looking up an order, a tracking status or a policy first.

Ask the vendor to show one case from start to finish, with the tool calls visible. If the system produced a fluent answer and made no lookups, it is generative AI with a new label.

Related: what is agentic AI and what is an AI agent. Tell us the job and the free proposal reveals which parts need an agent and which do not, within two working days.

Forget Mayo: Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad (Hint: It's Egg Free)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (445 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy.
  • According to recent reports, toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify.
  • But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy. But if you like a bit of garlic in yours, then toum — a Lebanese spread as rich in flavor as it is in fluffiness — is the answer you've been looking for.

According to recent reports, toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify. Far lighter in texture than mayonnaise but not quite as airy as whipped cream, it's a perfect middle ground that imparts serious flavor to fish. While it won't have quite the same richness as mayonnaise, since it lacks eggs, this can actually work in your favor. It gives your final product a lighter flavor profile that's highly conducive to other simple ways to level up tuna salad, such as adding horseradish or capers. It's perfect for when you want a protein-laden lunch that doesn't feel too heavy and won't leave you in need of a nap.

Served cold, it's delicious. But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else. The pungent notes fill your nostrils and blend with cheeses and toasted bread to create something as satisfying as any cheeseburger. Just be careful not to let any fall out, as toum's oil-based emulsion can separate or scorch when exposed to excessive heat.

It has been revealed that if you like a denser tuna salad, one packed with hearty chunks and thick vegetables, then mixing in a dollop of toum and calling it a day works just fine. However, if you want something quite light and creamy, almost like a tonnato sauce, then you need some high-powered beating action. By adding the toum and tuna to a stand mixer or a bowl with an electric hand mixer, you shred the fish into fine pieces. This allows the fluffy nature of the garlic spread to almost suspend the protein, giving the illusion of increased volume without actually adding any additional ingredients.

Toum can be quite acidic depending on the brand and recipe, and the lemon juice can quickly work with any pickles or relish to make your tuna salad a bit overpowering. To avoid anything too intense, you may want to switch to sweeter varieties. Still, if you're a diehard believer in acidic additions, apples, hot honey (a true kitchen multitasker), or a pinch of sugar can all help balance acidity quite well and add little nuances of their own that work well with garlic.

#46418. MVP Development Process: How Dubai Teams Validate Custom Software & AI Workflows

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (647 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

MVP Development Process: How Dubai Teams Validate Custom Software & AI Workflows

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When product and engineering teams initiative a newly introduced build in Dubai, it is easy to jump straight into writing code, setting up cloud infrastructure, or wiring up AI models before locking down the actual MVP development process.
  • A disciplined MVP development process keeps early builds focused on real workflow validation while laying clean foundations for custom software and AI capabilities later.
  • Industry observers note that before setting up repositories, choosing frameworks, or debating architecture, narrow the initial scope to one high-friction user or operational flow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When product and engineering teams initiative a newly introduced build in Dubai, it is easy to jump straight into writing code, setting up cloud infrastructure, or wiring up AI models before locking down the actual MVP development process. In a fast-moving market like Dubai and the wider UAE, teams feel constant pressure to ship quickly. Yet starting without a clear sequence often leads to bloated scope, slow feedback loops, and weeks of engineering hours spent on screens or features that users rarely touch.

A disciplined MVP development process keeps early builds focused on real workflow validation while laying clean foundations for custom software and AI capabilities later. Instead of treating launch as the finish line, it treats the first release as a structured test of real user behavior, operational fit, and product direction.

Industry observers note that before setting up repositories, choosing frameworks, or debating architecture, narrow the initial scope to one high-friction user or operational flow. Trying to solve every persona or edge case in version one usually blurs what you are actually trying to learn.

Industry observers note that when the primary workflow is sharply defined, every sprint has a clear purpose. Teams spend less time guessing which feature might impress stakeholders and more time testing whether the core problem is truly solved.

It has been revealed that early builds do not need heavy enterprise architecture on day one, nor should they ignore real data structures, security basics, or workflow constraints. Teams working on custom software in Dubai often see much better results when they separate quick validation slices from longer-term production modules:.

It has been revealed that at ThinkShift, we work with founders and businesses in Dubai on structured validation and custom software builds so teams can test real product assumptions early and scale around proven workflows. In practice, pairing disciplined discovery with practical AI systems—such as the approaches behind PraxisAI, ThinkShift CX, and Caliber AI—helps keep early releases grounded in real operational needs rather than surface-level demos.

Once a working MVP is in front of people, treat early production data as a diagnostic tool rather than just a scoreboard. Real usage reveals where a workflow flows smoothly and where friction still hides.

Teams that skip this observation loop often over-invest in scaling an unvalidated workflow or under-invest in the exact step where consumers get stuck. Observing actual behavior keeps engineering effort tied to real outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that not every workflow needs custom engineering right away. Standard off-the-shelf tools can often handle basic internal tracking or early back-office steps while you test core assumptions. The shift toward custom software becomes much clearer when off-the-shelf tools force awkward workarounds, slow down customer-facing experiences, cannot support custom data or approval flows, or limit product differentiation as adoption grows.

According to recent reports, when that moment arrives, having already validated the core workflow saves significant time. You already know which steps matter most, which edge cases occur in practice, and where custom software or AI workflow automation will create lasting leverage. For teams looking into custom software development in Dubai, starting with clear workflow validation makes the transition from prototype to production far smoother.

Start by defining one core workflow and a measurable validation goal, build a focused end-to-end slice to test real usage, observe friction points and user behavior, and iterate before expanding feature scope.

Custom software makes sense when off-the-shelf tools force heavy workarounds, cannot handle specific workflows or integrations, or limit control over data flows, security rules, and product differentiation.

Introduce AI where it solves a concrete bottleneck—such as classifying, summarizing, extracting, or routing information—paired with clear guardrails, fallback paths, and human handoffs for uncertain cases.

Teams often try to cover every user segment, edge case, and secondary feature upfront to feel "complete," which delays real-world testing and increases the risk of building features people do not prioritize.

What It Means When You Hear A Cowbell Ring At McDonald's

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mcDonald's is one of the biggest chains in the world, so being curious about what goes on behind the scenes is only natural.
  • To get to the bottom of this, Food Republic reached out to sisters Melissa Montes Blanco and Kristina Montes, third-generation owners and operators of several McDonald's locations.
  • As of writing, the Quarter Pounder is McDonald's only burger made with fresh, never-frozen beef.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mcDonald's is one of the biggest chains in the world, so being curious about what goes on behind the scenes is only natural. People love to throw around wild theories (no, the chicken nuggets aren't made from pink slime), but there are plenty of factual goings-on that might surprise fans. For instance, many customers are shocked to learn that McDonald's cooks aren't flipping your patties, or that every time you order a Quarter Pounder, you're setting off a cowbell in the kitchen.

To get to the bottom of this, Food Republic reached out to sisters Melissa Montes Blanco and Kristina Montes, third-generation owners and operators of several McDonald's locations. According to them, the cowbell rings because the Quarter Pounder is cooked to order. "When you go through the [drive-thru] or [order] delivery, whenever the order comes in, we will hear a cowbell in the kitchen, and that signals to the team to drop the meat at that point," they explained.

As of writing, the Quarter Pounder is McDonald's only burger made with fresh, never-frozen beef. When preparing meat for the Big Mac or cheeseburger, the frozen patties are batch-cooked and left in heated holding cabinets, so they can be assembled in seconds. The Quarter Pounder is a slightly more involved process, so when a customer places an order, the crew needs to be ready to throw a patty on the grill. It doesn't help that the patty takes much longer to cook. According to McDonald's, a regular patty takes around 42 seconds on the grill, while a Quarter Pounder patty nearly triples that at 112 seconds (almost two minutes). Fast food is in the name, so speed is everything, and a cowbell is a pretty effective way to spring the crew into action. The Montes sisters went on to explain that this extra time may be why you're sometimes asked to pull forward and wait outside of the drive-thru queue.

In a recent development, mcDonald's has the inner workings of the fast food game down to a science, from sensors that alert employees when a car pulls into the drive-thru to smart weight-checking scales for delivery orders that compare the total weight of the bag against expected targets to flag missing items before it leaves the kitchen. Most of its stores operated like a well-oiled machine long before the fresh-beef Quarter Pounder was introduced in 2018, so are the cowbells really necessary? According to several employees, they're nothing more than a nuisance.

Recent findings suggest that the alarm is part of McDonald's Kitchen Video System (KVS), which functions as a replacement for paper tickets by showing orders on screen for the crew. Alerts have traditionally been beeps and buzzes, so employees were caught off guard when a cowbell joined the mix. After the fresh grill display was installed, one self-identified employee took to Reddit to share their candid thoughts, claiming that "[it was] driving virtually everyone bats." They added, "It plays [an] unbelievably grating and repetitive cowbell sample instead of something more to the point ... It's annoying as hell[,] and nobody likes it except for a single manager. I thought about doing everyone a favor and just unplugging the speakers." A quick scroll through the replies was enough to show that this employee was far from alone, with plenty of coworkers piling on to share their own cowbell horror stories.

Despite waves of employee complaints, the cowbells don't seem to be going anywhere. McDonald's hasn't publicly responded to the backlash, and a November 2026 TikTok from McDonald's franchisee and content creator McBossladi has those all-too-familiar cowbells ringing in the background.

  • In a recent development, were you aware that Culver's even had a Grilled Reuben Melt on its menu?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's hard to mess up a Reuben because the ingredients are so simple: corned beef, sliced thin, tangy sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Thousand Island dressing (or Russian), all of which are sandwiched between two pieces of sturdy rye bread. No matter where you get your Reuben from, it's safe to say there are typically no bad ones — just good, better, and best.

According to recent reports, to that end, Food Republic did the legwork and created a list of the top Reubens you can order from a chain, from customers' perspectives, and one of the entries actually comes from Culver's. The Midwestern favorite, better known for its unique ButterBurgers, apparently makes the best grilled version of the sandwich you can find.

In a recent development, were you aware that Culver's even had a Grilled Reuben Melt on its menu? Because for as many customers who sing its praises, there appear to be an equal number who didn't even know it was an option. But what an option it is; it's a classic version, with lightly toasted bread, piles of salty corned beef, and melty Swiss cheese made in Culver's home state of Wisconsin.

One Reddit user shouted out the sandwich, writing that it "matches or beats some of the ones that I've had at many diners." Another commenter remarked that Culver's "slaps in general[,] but this goes hard for a fast food Reuben." Meanwhile, yet another Redditor called it "the best thing on the menu and the best [Reuben] I've ever had.".

Recent findings suggest that one of the best things about Culver's menu is how customizable it is, and the Reuben is no different. Culver's maintains a fairly long list of toppings that you can add to your melt; one Reddit user claimed that "[grilled onions] and mushrooms are the easiest way to elevate the sandwiches," though keep in mind that you might have to request customizations in person because online ordering doesn't always have the option. You could also add raw onions for a sharper bite, lettuce for a little greenery, tomato for some extra umami flavor, and, for a small fee, some thick-cut bacon.

Another user suggested adding a burger patty to the sandwich, calling the addition "incredible." Finally, if you're not a huge fan of rye, you could also swap it out for sourdough (the melt would then actually more closely resemble the best non-traditional chain restaurant Reuben, found at Schlotzsky's Deli), or opt for its Kaiser bun, brioche roll, gluten-free bun if you have a wheat allergy.

Breaking: 12 Powdered Gravy Mixes, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • According to recent reports, as most pro home chefs will tell you, making gravy from scratch isn't exactly rocket science.
  • According to recent reports, even so, the kind of store-bought gravy mix you choose matters — after all, anything you're planning to drown your meat and taters in had better be good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

According to recent reports, as most pro home chefs will tell you, making gravy from scratch isn't exactly rocket science. With the help of a little flour, butter, and broth, you could be on your way to a delicious gravy in just a few minutes. Still, there may be times when you simply aren't feeling up to it — whether you've had a rough week or are drowning in to-dos, packets of powdered gravy mix can prove a simple, flavorful fix.

According to recent reports, even so, the kind of store-bought gravy mix you choose matters — after all, anything you're planning to drown your meat and taters in had better be good. That's why I decided to make it my mission to test some of the most popular powdered gravy options in my area in hopes of offering my honest opinion about which truly deserves a spot in your kitchen.

In the upcoming post, I'm giving a complete rundown of every store-bought powdered gravy mix I could find, including the pricing, size, and taste of each. Bear in mind that the details mentioned in this article are subject to change and that the gravy packet selection featured here may not be reflective of what's available in your area. With that, join me as I prepare, taste, and rank 12 store-bought powdered gravy mixes from worst to best.

Prices are as of the date of publication and may vary based on region.

Sources indicate that great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is a no-frills Walmart-branded product that is, surprisingly, one of the costlier options on the list when you consider its price per unit. Though tagged at only 92 cents per packet, each pack contains .87 ounces, meaning you'll pay roughly $1.06 per ounce of powdered gravy.

Sources indicate that great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is prepared using the standard 1 cup of water per 1 packet of mix, and its ingredients include monosodium glutamate (otherwise known as "MSG"), which may pose a problem for gravy lovers who may be sensitive to the ingredient. I tore open the packet, and its unappetizing, artificial smell hit me right away. Once cooked, the mixture turned creamy and thick, but its color seemed unnatural, especially when compared to homemade. I gave it a hesitant taste, and nope, not good — Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix tasted like stale chicken and literally made me gag.

Would I recommend purchasing Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix? No way. Not only does its bright yellow color not resemble any chicken gravy I've ever made, but the taste was barely tolerable. I'm sure you could try improving this store-bought gravy with Worcestershire sauce, but I say, if it's convenience you seek, there are other options more deserving of your coin than this one.

Industry observers note that I hate to have to rank yet another Great Value powdered gravy mix so close to the bottom of the list, but it simply cannot be helped. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix is a bit cheaper than its chicken-flavored counterpart — expect to pay 78 cents per .87 ounces, which works out to around 89.7 cents per ounce of powdered gravy. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix doesn't contain the MSG that the chicken flavor includes, but that doesn't mean I recommend purchasing it — like the former, it has a weird smell and taste that I simply can't get past.

I prepared Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix according to the package directions and watched it bubble and simmer on the stove. The mix eventually turned the typical light brown color normally associated with turkey gravy and had an uber-thick consistency. I let it cool slightly before giving it a quick taste — sadly, it had the same stomach-churning qualities as the previous flavor. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix tasted woefully artificial; in fact, the additives or chemicals present in the gravy were just about the only thing I could taste. Needless to say, I would never dish up Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix to guests at Thanksgiving — you'd be better off leaving not-so-Great Value picks like this one on the shelf.

In a recent development, before offering my opinion here, I have to be honest and say I'm not a person who prepares peppered gravy often. That said, I'm willing to bet Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix doesn't quite encapsulate its classic flavor the way other options do.

Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix costs $1.22 per 2.75 ounces, with a unit price of 44.4 cents per ounce. As is typical for many peppered gravy mixes on the market, this packet contains a little more powdered gravy mix per pack than other varieties and flavors. Its preparation requires more water, too — you'll need 1 ¾ cups this time around versus the usual 1 cup.

Recent findings suggest that southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix tasted annoyingly bland, with a flavor very similar to what you'd get if you added black pepper to plain cream. Though thick, it had no richness of flavor, and I couldn't imagine it doing much to elevate anyone's sausage gravy. I flipped the packet over and was surprised by what I saw on the ingredient list: Palm oil and modified food starch were the first ingredients mentioned, which is hardly a good way to start a high-quality gravy, if you ask me. As I remarked, I am by no means an expert in peppered gravy, but based on first impressions alone, I'd say skip this brand and opt for other, richer, more flavorful brands on the market.

If you're surprised to see McCormick Brown Gravy Mix ranked lower on the list, join the club. I, for one, adore brown gravy, and with McCormick being one of the most popular gravy and seasoning brands on the market, I figured I'd be in for a real treat. Expect to pay 97 cents for .87 ounces of it, making each ounce cost roughly $1.12.

In a recent development, when cooking up McCormick Brown Gravy Mix, I couldn't help but feel excited — its texture was thick and glossy, and the gravy had a deep brown hue that just screamed umami beef. It even had the savory, enticing aroma of a succulent pot roast, so imagine my surprise when I discovered the gravy tastes, quite literally, like nothing.

Sources indicate that that's right — McCormick Brown Gravy Mix features a flavor so weak I could barely taste anything at all. To think McCormick Brown Gravy Mix smelled and looked so great without delivering flavor even half of what was teased is mind-boggling. Needless to say, McCormick Brown Gravy Mix isn't worth the buy — I'd recommend picking up some beef broth and making your own simple brown gravy or choosing one of the higher-ranking varieties over this one.

Though not the best out there, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix is a dark horse in terms of taste and performance. The gravy comes sold in an .87-ounce pack and was priced at 83 cents, about 95 cents per ounce. It contains artificial ingredients along with a host of additives, but hey, if that kinda stuff doesn't bother you, feel free to ignore those stats.

According to recent reports, I went into my tasting of Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix with low expectations — almost every Amazon Grocery item I've sampled in the past left me underwhelmed. Much to my amazement, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix held its own in terms of consistency and aroma — it was a bit thinner than a few other options on the list, yes, but still managed to be just thick enough. I also found its glossy deep brown appearance mesmerizing, and its smell rich and meaty, just the way a good brown gravy should be.

Recent findings suggest that going in for a slurp, I didn't walk away disappointed — though the flavor was nowhere near as potent as its aroma, it was leaps and bounds better than McCormick. I could clearly taste its beefy notes, and its umami depth was decent overall. One thing I will say is that Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix tastes slightly watered down; still, I think it will get you by if you're looking for a tasty, inexpensive brown gravy to crown your mashers.

In a recent development, pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix is pretty good; though not a peppered gravy kinda gal, I have an appreciation for this brand and would recommend it over Southeastern Mills any day. This mix comes in a 2.75-ounce packet, only this time, you'll need to add 2 cups of water instead of the 1 ¾ cups Southeastern Mills requires. Each packet costs $1.33, meaning you'll cop this powdered peppered gravy for about 48.4 cents per ounce.

Recent findings suggest that when cooking up Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix, the first thing I noticed was its golden hue. The yellowish tinge of the Pioneer-branded gravy made it more attractive than the stark white presentation of Southeastern Mills. It was just as thick as the former brand, if not thicker, though whether or not its flavor would prove better was yet to be seen.

So, how'd Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix taste? Though I still consider its flavor mundane compared to traditional chicken or brown gravies, Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix had more depth than Southeastern Mills. It's not listed in the ingredients, but there seemed to be a hint of butter flavor in the mixture — this deepened the taste and added complexity. All in all, if I were to grab a packet of peppered gravy for breakfast, this is the brand I'd get — not only does it look better, but its taste is pretty decent, too.

Sources indicate that mcCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix wasn't too bad — it isn't something I'd choose over homemade gravy for Thanksgiving dinner, but it's good if you're in a pinch and want something cheap. The gravy comes sold in a .87-ounce packet for $1.63, and while this might not sound super expensive, it's actually a little pricier than others, at $1.87 per ounce.

According to recent reports, mcCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix yields a light brown color I found fitting for turkey gravy — it certainly looked the part, featuring a medium-thick consistency and glossy appearance. McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix has a poultry-like flavor that's pleasing but leans more chicken than turkey in my opinion. Nevertheless, I consider this turkey gravy option to be one of the punchier, more robust picks out there, and though I don't necessarily consider it holiday worthy, it might be good to have a packet or two in your pantry for days when you're low on time.

Fire & Smoke Society Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix is a super unique option, and though I probably wouldn't buy it again, you might consider trying it if you're looking to sample something outside of the norm. The packaging here has the kind of aesthetic that makes you think it's fancy by looks alone — its price also stands out, at $1.72 per 1-ounce pack, working out to $1.72 per ounce. A quick scan of the ingredients reveals several surprises — though not a clean ingredient pick by any means, some additions — like cumin, chili powder, and even coffee — left me curious as to what kind of flavor I was in for.

I prepared the gravy as per its 1 cup to 1 packet instructions and immediately noticed a difference in its texture compared to the others. Fire & Smoke Society Major Sunday Brown Gravy Mix yields a thinner, silkier texture than most. Its aroma was totally unexpected, as it was more akin to grill spices than savory beef. After tasting Fire & Smoke Society's Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix, I found myself torn — the taste wasn't gross, but didn't encompass the type of flavor I expect from a classic brown gravy.

Industry observers note that is Fire & Smoke Society Massive Sunday Brown Gravy Mix good? Yes! Would I buy it again? Probably not. Blame it on my traditional taste buds, but for me, this powdered gravy mix is just OK.

According to recent reports, is there a difference between country and peppered gravy? Apparently, there is, and as it stands, I prefer the former. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was a breath of fresh air flavor-wise, but I suppose that isn't surprising given I love practically anything that the Kinder brand produces. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was priced at $1.72 per 1.9 ounces at my local Walmart, working out to about 90.5 cents per ounce.

Sources indicate that kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was truly phenomenal in terms of taste and texture. First and foremost, the gravy recommends preparing it with 2 cups of milk, which automatically gave it a richer, sweeter finish. Once cooked, the gravy was thick and featured a stark white appearance flecked with tons of contrasting black pepper throughout.

Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning tastes almost identical to creamy, buttery, garlicky mashed potatoes, no spuds needed. I'd imagine this would taste incredible paired with creamy taters, and I wouldn't hesitate to dish it up as a turkey topper during the holidays. As if things couldn't get better, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning uses fairly clean ingredients, with nowhere near as much of the ick featured in other powdered gravy mixes on the list. With all things considered, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning is one of my favorite powdered gravy mixes on the market.

Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix costs $1.72 for .85 ounces making it one of the most expensive powdered gravy mixes on the market at $2.02 per ounce. It's the only gluten-free organic chicken option on the list, and I honestly didn't expect it to taste as good as it did. Not that I have anything against organic foods — I actually love them and find the use of minimal ingredients refreshing. Still, in the world of gravy, I guess I just didn't expect a natural option like this one to hold its own when pitted against others containing various flavor-boosting additives. Thankfully, this humble pick from Simply Organic proved me wrong.

According to recent reports, simply Organic chicken gravy calls for the standard 1 cup of gravy packet seasoning per 1 cup of water. As it cooked, it began to take on a sauce-like consistency that was thick, glossy, and light brown. I gave it a taste and was floored — this organic pick boasted a flavor way better than any other store-bought chicken gravy I've tried.

It has been revealed that simply Organic chicken gravy had a bold, savory, and garlicky flavor beautifully enhanced with prominent notes of celery seed. Thus, though expensive, you can rest assured that your money is going to good use — Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix is a phenomenal replacement for homemade when you don't feel like whipping up chicken gravy on your own.

Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is the only organic brown gravy on the list, and let me tell you, it did not disappoint. Unlike its chicken-flavored predecessor, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is slightly cheaper, at 1 ounce for $1.72 ( $1.72 per ounce). Being the organic grab that it is, expect Simply Organic brown gravy to be non-GMO and free of artificial colors, flavors, and ingredients. One of its best attributes is its use of cornstarch rather than flour, as this makes it a great option for people looking to ditch wheat.

Industry observers note that I was delighted to find Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix packing so much flavor — after the previous brown gravy duds, I didn't have much hope that there was a truly good packaged option out there. In truth, Simply Organic's brown gravy is one of the most flavorful in its class — it was one of the few to truly capture the beefy, oniony savor I come to expect from a good homemade brown gravy.

One thing to note is that Simply Organic brown gravy has a medium consistency and a color a lot lighter than others in its category. Still, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix would make the perfect companion to roast beef or over creamy mashed potatoes, and I doubt anyone would be able to detect the difference between it and homemade.

In a recent development, yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is unlike any other gravy I've tried — I had never sampled jalapeño gravy before, nor did I know it existed. Now that it's on my radar, in my cabinet it will stay. It's really that good, even if it is $2.50 per 2.82-ounce packet (89 cents per ounce)!

Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy contains no artificial flavors, which to me is pretty impressive. Though not gluten-free like the aforementioned Simply Organic picks, it does at least contain fewer additives while still managing to achieve unbelievably thick results. You only need to use 2 cups of water per packet to cash in on this irresistibly luscious golden gravy; its texture was so rich and smooth my mouth watered just at the sight of it.

Aside from its tantalizing consistency, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy tastes incredible — I'd describe its flavor as similar to high-quality jalapeño nacho cheese, but with less emphasis on the cheese. It's quite spicy, and though not unbearably so, still isn't something I'd recommend offering to kids. All in all, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is an amazing option I'd buy over and over again — try it on fried chicken cutlets, potatoes, stuffing, or hot sandwiches. Yum!

Sources indicate that the 12 powdered gravy mixes selected for this article were chosen based on availability in my area, with most sourced from Walmart and Amazon. Each gravy mix was ranked primarily based on texture and flavor, although other factors, like ingredients and pricing, were considered. As always, pricing and availability are subject to change.

The Egg McMuffin Order You Can Only Find In Canada

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

McDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu. Alongside familiar faves, you'll find items Americans can't order, the most envy-inducing among them arguably being the Egg BLT McMuffin. Once you hear what's in it, don't be surprised if you catch yourself planning a trip to our northern neighbor.

Industry observers note that the Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin. A second version uses nearly identical ingredients but swaps the whole leaves for shredded lettuce. You can only get this variation at McDonald's restaurants located inside Walmart stores — part of a decades-old partnership that once placed roughly 1,000 outposts in the retail chain. McDonald's later closed hundreds of them as drive-thrus became the main source of sales, though Walmart continues to host many locations in Canada.

According to recent reports, to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative. Your best bet is to start with a Bacon, Egg & Cheese McMuffin, which already ticks off half the ingredients. Ask for a touch of mayo, which gets you close to the sauce of the Canadian original. Since lettuce and tomatoes are lunchtime items, your odds improve near the end of breakfast hours when stores are prepping the lunch menu — you'll likely have to order them at the counter or window.

The Egg BLT might have already convinced you to add McDonald's to your itinerary next time you're in Canada, but it's not the only breakfast item worth the detour. One that caught our eye was the Mighty McGriddles. While the U.S. offers the Bacon, Egg & Cheese and Sausage, Egg & Cheese varieties separately, the Canadian version puts both to shame by stacking a double helping of hickory-smoked bacon, a sausage patty, egg, and cheese between two maple-flavored griddle cakes — a gloriously overstuffed creation that lives up to its name. The Mighty McMuffin follows the same logic, coming loaded with both meats for anyone who can never decide between the two.

Another familiar face on Canadian McDonald's breakfast menus is the bagel, though while America only offers plain, Canada also serves sesame and everything varieties. You can even order one toasted with butter or Philadelphia cream cheese — widely known as the best store-bought brand — as if you're at a proper bagel shop.

Recent findings suggest that canada's McDonald's restaurants aren't afraid to put a twist on U.S. staples, and they also introduce new items altogether. You won't find chicken anywhere on the standard U.S. breakfast menu, which makes the Chicken McGriddles feel like a curveball up north. The simple yet delicious sandwich pairs a breaded chicken patty with two sweet, maple-flavored griddle cakes for some serious sweet-and-savory fusion.

#46394. How I Get Free Traffic from ChatGPT in 2025 (AIO vs SEO)

📅 04 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 79m • 📚 Deep Dive (15868 w)
