📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Recent findings suggest that the actual difference between a hamburger and a steakburger comes down to the quality of meat used in the grind, but the difference between a homemade steakburger and one from a steakhouse is all about a lighter texture. Melissa Clark, author of "The Massive Book of Dinner: Recipes and Rules (and How to Break Them)," tells us that achieving that characteristic is quite easy if you use ground cracker crumbs.

"Any kind of cracker or breadcrumbs will make a burger lighter," Clark notes. "Ritz and saltines work really well. They are very airy, which helps lighten the ground meat." Beef is rather dense, even if you avoid overworking it into a firm, puck-like consistency that's more similar to sausage than a tender patty. But a quarter cup of ground crackers per pound of meat can make a world of difference.

When meat cooks, it contracts and releases juice and fat. Crackers, however, absorb them rather than allowing them to seep out of the patty, preventing it from shriveling up too much. Since steakhouse burgers typically use thick patties, this also keeps them nice and moist. Whereas a thin sliver of well-crusted beef may be just what you want in a smashburger, retaining moisture is a vital component to keeping your steakhouse burgers not only light, but also at their peak flavor.

Sources indicate that using plain, unsalted crackers can still keep your steakhouse burgers light, but it would be a missed opportunity for better flavor. While you also don't want to use something starch-free, like a nut- or seed-based variety, Melissa Clark is a substantial believer in picking a tasty brand and smashing them up properly.

"Using crackers can add great flavor – Ritz, with their butteriness, are especially lovely," Clark explains. Flavorful but unobtrusive, Ritz crackers are the perfect addition to any savory dish because just about everything can benefit from their toasty richness. But if you want to get a bit experimental, you can also just as easily use Cheez-Its or anything seasoned. This is an easy way to avoid coming up with a specialty spice blend since you'll be adding enough to thoroughly flavor your meat.

Recent findings suggest that clark is also a proponent of using whatever method you can to grind the crackers into a fine powder. "Grind the crackers in a food processor, blender or tuck them in a plastic bag and crush them under a rolling pin," she added. Large chunks can make some bites unexpectedly soggy and, if using a seasoned cracker, a little too flavorful. Plus, if some parts of your blend don't have a starch, they may end up expressing their juices too much, leaving some bites juicy and light and others dense and dry.

#46376. REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2875 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blogspot ↗ Open Full Page

REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?
  • What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?
  • In a recent development, you use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code? You use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A upcoming open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today. In this guide The problem with reverse engineering How REA solves it How REA works What REA can analyze Real examples How to get started REA at a glance Using REA responsibly Frequently asked questions The Problem: Reverse Engineering Is Hard Reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles. 1. A steep learning curve Reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result. 2. Too many tools and no single workflow An Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks. 3. Slow, manual investigation Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature. 4. AI answers you cannot verify If you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real. 5. Painful setup Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break. The Solution: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above. The Problem How REA Solves It Steep learning curve You ask in plain English. Your agent runs the tools and explains the results. Too many tools One MCP server covers native binaries, Electron apps, Android, .NET, websites, and dozens of other formats. Slow and manual The agent traces code, references, and calls for you. Answers you cannot verify Every result includes the evidence and limitations behind it. Painful setup One command registers REA with your agent and backs up your existing configuration. You do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer. How REA Works You ask a question. For example, how a feature in a particular app works. The agent calls REA. It uses MCP to inspect the target and trace the relevant code. REA returns findings. These include code, references, and clearly marked unknowns. The agent acts on them. It can explain the behavior, ask follow-up questions, or write and test its own version of the feature. The same workflows are available from the terminal, so you can also script them without an agent. Analysis runs locally on your machine. Your agent receives the tool results, and your AI provider’s own data policy applies to that part. What Can REA Analyze? The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups. Native programs and binaries REA returns pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls, and references. Deep native analysis uses an engine you already have, such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna. It also supports GNU objdump and Rizin for offline inspection. JavaScript and Electron apps This is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships. Android apps and devices REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too. .NET and managed code For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program. Websites and network captures REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads. Specialist formats The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. Most of these use built-in static inspection, so no extra software is required. Real Examples: What Has REA Done? The project publishes several case studies on its website. DX-Ball sound panning. REA followed a sound call into a helper function and turned incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passed 3,205 test cases against the original x86 code and matched all 63 compiled function bytes. Notion’s clipboard bridge. REA traced how Notion’s Electron app moves clipboard data from the renderer through preload and IPC into the main process, including the rich clipboard format. TH04 bullet patterns. REA recovered the angle calculations of a classic DOS game and compared the rebuilt C++ with the original compiler output. Bonus: build RL environments from a web app REA can record a web app session and turn its API calls into tools an AI agent can use. It then exports a runnable environment for reinforcement learning or for testing how well an agent completes tasks. With a saved HAR file, the command looks like this: rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json You then run the result with AgentEnv and Docker, and add your own tasks and reward checks. How to Get Started With REA You need Node.js and npm. The project lists supported Node versions as 22.x (22.23.4 or newer), 24.x (24.22.1 or newer), or 26.12.1 and above. Step 1: Run the setup command npx rea-agents setup Step 2: Choose your agents and approve the changes Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents. It shows you the proposed changes first and keeps backups of your existing configuration. Step 3: Restart your agent The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again. Step 4: Ask your first question Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. Prefer the terminal? You can inspect an extracted Electron app or ASAR file directly: npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json To keep REA installed, run npm install --global rea-agents. REA changes rapidly, so use rea upgrade to stay current. Updating is also the first fix to try if you run into a bug. REA at a Glance What makes it special REA combines the reach of dozens of analysis tools with the convenience of an AI agent. It helps you understand software you do not have source code for, and it backs each conclusion with evidence instead of guesses. The range of supported formats, from native binaries to Electron apps to Android devices, is unusually broad for a free tool. Key features Works through MCP with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents Evidence and limitations attached to every result Local analysis on your own machine A full command-line interface for scripting Support for dozens of file and app types An RL environment builder Guides and case studies on the official website Pricing REA itself: free and open source (MIT license) Commercial engines such as IDA Pro, Hopper, and JEB: you must obtain these legally under their own licenses Ghidra: a free option for native analysis; see the setup guide for details Perfect for Developers, security researchers, students, software preservationists, and anyone who wants to understand how an app works. Using REA Responsibly Use REA only on software you own or are authorized to examine. The project is intended for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you have permission to study. It does not permit cracked tools, stolen license keys, or bypassing license restrictions. Read the project’s disclaimer before you start. Also be careful where you download it from. The project warns that a similar repository name or a copied README does not make a download official. Use only these sources: GitHub: github.com/morluto/rea Website: rea.tools npm package: rea-agents Frequently Asked Questions Do I need Hopper or Ghidra? Only for deep native binary analysis. JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native engine, and setup can install Hopper with your approval. Does REA upload my app? No. Analysis runs locally. Your agent sees the results, and its provider has its own data policy. Which AI agents work with REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers can use it. What should I do if I find a bug? Update first, because a recent release may already include the fix. If the problem continues, open an issue on GitHub with your REA version, the target type, the steps to reproduce, and the error output. Final Thoughts The old problem was simple: understanding software without source code took too much skill, too many tools, and too much time. REA’s answer is just as simple. It gives your AI agent the tools to investigate, and it requires the agent to show its evidence. What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?

In a recent development, you use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A newly introduced open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today.

It has been revealed that reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles.

In a recent development, reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result.

Sources indicate that an Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks.

Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature.

Sources indicate that if you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real.

Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break.

REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above.

It has been revealed that you do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer.

The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups.

Industry observers note that this is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships.

REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too.

For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program.

REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads.

The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again.

Among the most iconic Middle Eastern dishes, hummus blends chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice, and optional seasonings to delicious effect. It's a dish that can be assembled at home, but many tasty store-bought versions are available, too. If your grocery store hummus happens to taste a little flat, though, reach for toum. Just a spoonful of this condiment will make a version that's 10 times better.

Hailing from Lebanon, toum is an emulsion made by blending a generous dose of garlic with oil, lemon juice, and sometimes water. Smooth and airy in texture yet with an underlying bite, it lends hummus a dose of garlicky goodness and acidity, readily transforming a bland flavor into a complex one. Plus, the condiment packs in extra fat, helping to improve the perceived creaminess of disappointingly dry hummus. Since toum is a homogeneous paste, it's easy to incorporate, and its flavor can be less aggressive than raw garlic, too.

Sources indicate that you won't need much toum to make an impact. Start by mixing in just under a teaspoon per standard 8-ounce container, then work in gradual increments from there. For ease, grab a jar of toum online, or peruse the same grocery aisles where you bought the hummus. You could also easily prep your own toum in bulk — the condiment typically keeps for up to a month in the fridge.

It has been revealed that A toum-inflected hummus makes a great dip, scooped up with za'atar-dusted pita chips, pretzels, veggie chips, or whatever other crisp your heart desires. Note that there are many other ways to use hummus in everyday cooking, though — especially when it's mixed with toum.

According to recent reports, for example, consider topping the condiment with spiced ground beef or lamb, a popular Middle Eastern combination. Flavor the minced meat with earthy spices and fiery chilies, and the garlicky hummus makes for a mouthwatering flavor combo, turning the store-bought dip into an extra-hearty meal.

Industry observers note that alternatively, make the chickpea-based dip less of a centerpiece and use it as a sandwich spread instead — it would pair delectably with crunchy vegetables like cucumbers and onions, as well as greens like spinach. Served on whole-grain bread, the dip makes for a delicious vegetarian meal.

Looking for an extra creative twist? You could even use the toum hummus to make your next batch of tuna salad — the garlicky flavor will pair terrifically with the tinned fish. When you're craving Middle Eastern flavors but don't feel like cooking, keep the toum-hummus pairing in mind.

5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
  • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
  • One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:.

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:.

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is vital for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”.

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

The essence of the best grilled cheese lies in the delicious combination of melted cheese and crisped bread. There are many methods to accomplish such a pairing, with plenty of tips to give you the best results imaginable. If you're after a version that's especially ooey-gooey, try making the sandwich with cheddar cheese spread.

Available from several brands at widespread grocery stores like Walmart, cheddar cheese spread is essentially cheddar mixed with butter. The foodstuff is easily spreadable on bread and melts when it's heated, making a grilled cheese with a pleasantly runny interior. While it's creamier than classic cheddar, the flavor is no afterthought, with this cheese's sharpness still perceptible.

In a recent development, using butter alongside cheese is common in grilled cheese recipes; the spread lets you conveniently lather on both components at once. The fat enhances the bread's crispiness, all while retaining a moist interior. As a sole filling, the spread turns the dish luxuriously decadent — but complemented with a few slices of cheese, it's a grilled cheese rendition to remember.

There are many international grilled cheese styles to explore; cheddar cheese spread fits into a wide range of renditions. Combined with a store-bought loaf of sourdough and sliced cheddar, the spread makes a mouth-watering classic. However, you can consider layering in other ingredients, too — thereby making a cheddar grilled cheese with a twist.

In a recent development, for example, the cheese's sharpness welcomes a sweet contrast. Spread a jam or jelly into the sandwich, whether a rich fig jam, tart cranberry preserves, or a sweet blackberry jam. For a sweet touch with less sugar, you could also use fresh fruits to upgrade any grilled cheese; the spread would go great with apples, for example, as apples and cheddar are a match made in sandwich heaven. And you could also consider leaning into the spice, smearing on spicy brown mustard or hot pepper jelly for a light dose of heat.

Consider trying out other ingredient add-ins, too. Caramelized onions will lend a grilled cheese a subtle nutty sweetness, while bacon bits bring a savory touch. Cheddar cheese spreads allow the many different flavors to come together, letting you easily craft a sandwich to your tastes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that turkey, ham, mashed potatoes, casseroles, pumpkin, cranberries, stuffing ... the annual fall-flavored feast that we know and love is always a crowd-pleasing holiday meal to look forward to. And one of the best things about Thanksgiving isn't just the meal itself; it's all of the delicious leftovers that inevitably follow.

Especially when you're hosting a crowd (which is possible to do stress-free with these tips from Guy Fieri), those leftovers can be abundant. But the beauty is that there's so much more you can do with your Thanksgiving leftovers than just reheat and re-eat. From soups, sandwiches, and snacks that repurpose your ingredients to completely latest dishes that transform the original elements of the meal, you can take those leftovers in so many directions.

If you're looking for new ideas or creative ways to use up what's left in the fridge, we've got a plethora of recipes to try that'll help you make the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. (Pro tip: Just don't forget the 2-2-2 rule with your leftovers to ensure food safety.).

Sources indicate that whether you enjoyed some mac & cheese on Thanksgiving Day or not, this recipe is a whole new twist on the classic that infuses the beloved dish with holiday flavor. It's honestly a little shocking how many leftover ingredients manage to make their way into this one recipe, but when you think about it ... how could it not taste good?

Sources indicate that this Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese incorporates three different types of cheese — fontina, cheddar, and mascarpone — to make the cheese sauce. Then come the Thanksgiving leftovers that get folded into the dish: shredded turkey meat, sweet potatoes, peas, and pasta. After it's baked, the whole thing is topped off with some cranberry sauce to bring the Thanksgiving flavors home.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese.

Recent findings suggest that now, this is a fun one — it's Thanksgiving dinner in burger form! Not only can you use that leftover stuffing, but this recipe also calls for turkey meat, gravy, and cranberry sauce, so this one wins for maximizing whatever's taking up space in the fridge. And it's incredibly tasty, too.

Sources indicate that the "burger" is a combination of stuffing, turkey, eggs, and milk in patty form. The patty is then griddled in some butter and topped off with cranberry sauce, gravy, and goat cheese to create a burger that'll leave you stuffed in the best way.

Recipe: Leftover Thanksgiving Stuffing Burger.

Okay, a turkey cheesesteak might seem a little contradictory, but this one's worth entertaining when it comes to making the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. You won't just knock out the leftover turkey, but also any leftover gravy with this Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak.

It has been revealed that the cheesesteak starts with sautéed sweet onions, and then the turkey (dark meat works great if you have it), gravy, and cornichons are added to the mix before two types of cheese (provolone and American cheese) are melted on top. Everything is stuffed into toasty hoagie rolls to make a saucy, messy, tasty Thanksgiving cheesesteak.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak.

Why not whip up the ultimate comfort meal to enjoy the weekend after Thanksgiving? Once the holiday winds down, you can use your leftover turkey (and any extra pumpkin puree you might have lying around) in this Pumpkin and Turkey Chili recipe. This fall take on a classic slow cooker chili recipe incorporates pumpkin puree into the stew along with a blend of warm spices like cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg.

To sub in your already-cooked turkey, just skip the initial step where you'd brown the ground turkey, and instead add some cubed or shredded turkey once your chili is simmering.

Recipe: Pumpkin and Turkey Chili.

Making croquettes is a fun and delicious way to use up that leftover turkey. Croquettes actually originated in France as a way to use up leftover meats and vegetables, so they're the perfect way to repurpose those Thanksgiving leftovers.

The cheesy croquettes are made by sautéeing mushrooms, onions, and garlic and combining the mixture with cooked turkey, parsley, and mozzarella cheese. They're then shaped into balls, dipped into egg and breadcrumbs, and lightly fried until golden brown and crispy.

Recipe: Crispy Turkey and Cheese Croquettes.

Shepherd's pie is a great follow-up recipe to Thanksgiving if you need a way to reuse copious amounts of mashed potatoes, because that iconic mashed potato topping makes shepherd's pie what it is. This particular recipe is made with ground lamb and vegetables like corn, peas, and carrots as the base of the pie, but you could easily sub in your leftover turkey as well if you want to knock out two leftovers in one go.

Industry observers note that either way, this Simple Shepherd's Pie is even easier to make since the mashed potatoes are already done. All you need to do is assemble, bake, and enjoy ... or if you're feeling ambitious, you can try one of these 15 secret ingredients to make your Shepherd's Pie the best it can be.

Bought too many potatoes on your Thanksgiving grocery run? This casserole will come in handy for those extra ingredients. The simple, easy-to-make dish combines potatoes, onions, bacon, and thyme with cream, chicken stock, and cheese. Everything gets baked until it's melty and delicious, making a perfect side dish to pair with any leftover meat from the holiday.

This recipe uses blue cheese, which complements the bacon, but you can feel free to use any cheese you like (cheddar, mozzarella, or even Gruyère would all work great).

Recipe: Potato Bacon Cheese Bake.

According to recent reports, this comforting soup brings together many ingredients that were most likely on your Thanksgiving shopping list, including carrots, apples, potatoes, and pecans. It's the perfect meal to throw together that'll make use of all of those extra groceries that you're not sure what to do with. Carrots and apples may not be your first thoughts as the base of a soup, but trust us, this comforting soup recipe is a (somewhat unexpected) winner.

Sources indicate that all you need to do is cook your vegetables down with plenty of flavorful herbs and spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, and fresh thyme. Add your stock, blend until smooth, and finish off with the cream for a nutty and rich yet soothing soup that you can work your way through all week.

Recipe: Nutty Carrot and Apple Soup.

According to recent reports, for all those who may have purchased some fresh pumpkins for your Thanksgiving pie but didn't get around to using all of it, we've got just the recipe. As a bonus, it'll use up those extra potatoes, too!

Put a fall spin on a classic potato gratin by slicing your pumpkin into pieces or rounds the same size as your potatoes. The cream mixture, which is made up of heavy cream, garlic, thyme, rosemary, and salt, gets layered with your pumpkin and potatoes; then everything is covered with grated Swiss cheese and baked longer than you may think until the whole dish is bubbly, browned, and cheesy.

Recipe: Herbed Pumpkin Potato Gratin.

According to recent reports, whether you've got some extra sweet potatoes lying around from a casserole side dish or a sweet potato pie, this Sweet Potato Tarte Tatin is a delicious way to use them up. And with a little puff pastry, this dish looks impressive but doesn't take long to make a classic tarte tatin.

Sources indicate that the trick is making the caramel element; once you've gotten that down, the rest is smooth sailing. Your homemade caramel will come together with sliced sweet potatoes and a puff pastry covering to produce an irresistible starchy take on the tarte tatin.

Recipe: Sweet Potato Tarte Tatin.

In a recent development, similar to the tarte tatin, you can use a store-bought dough (this time, paper-thin Greek phyllo pastry) to keep this dessert simple. Baklava is typically made with nuts, but this recipe replaces that crunchy ingredient with a smooth pumpkin puree — along with spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove — for a tasty fall twist on this decadent, flaky treat.

Industry observers note that baklava involves making a simple syrup of sorts, and then it's all about layering (and this hack for assembling can make your baklava process even quicker). In the end, you'll have an extremely crispy, sweet-yet-spiced dessert born from leftover pumpkin puree.

If there's one thing you may not have thought to do with your leftover pumpkin and cranberries, it might be homemade liqueur. It might seem a little extreme, but it's not as complicated as it sounds, and you will be rewarded with an ingredient that'll help level up your baking and cocktails for many weeks to come.

It has been revealed that in short, the process just involves cooking down your chosen ingredient with sugar, then adding a high-proof liquor like vodka, and then straining it and letting it sit. That's it!

Recipe: Cranberry Liqueur and Pumpkin Liqueur.

According to recent reports, if you didn't quite make as much apple pie filling as you planned, don't worry — this one's for you. It's basically a shortcut apple pie filling that you can throw on some ice cream, douse in whipped cream, or simply enjoy on its own.

Industry observers note that this Sweet Spiced Baked Apples recipe is one of the easiest ways to make use of all of those leftover apples. Any apples will do: Honeycrisp, Fuji, Pink Lady, you name it. All you need to do is bake them with an undeniably delicious mixture of brown sugar, walnuts, butter, and spices. It's so simple, and so satisfying.

Recipe: Sweet Spiced Baked Apples.

Sources indicate that sticking with those leftover apples, this recipe will make a fantastic breakfast or brunch in the days following Thanksgiving. The Americanized origins of Dutch baby pancakes are a bit complicated, but long story short, this creation is essentially a giant, skillet-baked pancake. And it's a great go-to dish to capitalize on your extra apples, because you most likely have everything else you need stocked in your kitchen.

This Dutch baby recipe uses a batter made of flour, milk, eggs, honey, vanilla extract, salt, and melted butter. Next, pour the batter over thinly sliced apples that have been tossed in brown sugar and cinnamon. Everything is then baked together to perfection until your leftover apples turn into puffy, golden goodness.

Recent findings suggest that this is a unique and flavorful way to use any extra pumpkins you have from the holiday. The bonus? The presentation is impressive, so if you find yourself continuing to host through the weekend, this is another great meal to provide for your guests that will help you repurpose some of your Thanksgiving ingredients.

In a recent development, with everything from coconut milk and ground pork to ginger, soy sauce, and water chestnuts, this rice dish includes a lot of really interesting ingredients that may not seem like they belong together, but they all unite to build a warm, aromatic meal. Just trust the process, serve it up inside a pumpkin, and watch your guests marvel.

Recipe: Stuffed Pumpkin With Aromatic Rice.

Although this recipe includes a lot of similar ingredients as the above (rice, pumpkin, nuts), the elements come together in a totally different way to create a totally different dish: a warmly spiced, sweet rice pudding that'll taste just like your Thanksgiving pumpkin pie.

The dessert is made with Arborio rice, almond milk, maple syrup, pumpkin puree, vanilla, and spices — everything gets simmered together until it thickens into a pudding, then chilled and served with glazed pecans for extra crunch.

Recipe: Vegan Pumpkin Pecan Rice Pudding.

Leftovers truly shine when you use them to build a great sandwich. Meet this Sweet and Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich, which can be made with your leftover Thanksgiving turkey and ham. In addition to the sliced duo of meat, this sandwich features Gruyère cheese, mayo, and raspberry jam (although you can obviously sub in some cranberry sauce if you so please), all stacked between slices of brioche bread.

What makes this Monte Cristo extra delicious is the French toast treatment that it gets: Once assembled, the entire sandwich is dipped in a mixture of egg, half-and-half, and nutmeg and lightly fried in butter until golden brown. Oh, it's then topped off with some powdered sugar for good measure.

Recipe: Sweet And Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich.

Here's another fun breakfast recipe to keep things interesting over the holiday weekend! This take on a Croque Madame (a classic French sandwich typically made with ham, cheese, and Mornay sauce and topped with a sunny-side-up egg) creates a "waffled" version of the sandwich by employing a waffle iron as the cooking tool.

In a recent development, where do the leftovers come in? The waffle "batter" is made with your leftover Thanksgiving stuffing, which you'll then combine with milk and eggs. This concoction is then topped with slices of ham and grated cheddar cheese, and finished off with a fried or poached egg. Post-Thanksgiving brunch is served.

If you've still got some sweet potatoes left from your holiday shopping, this is another great recipe to make use of them — and it couldn't be simpler. This Sweet Potato and Sausage Hash makes a great breakfast or brunch, and can be topped with some eggs or eaten on its own. And all it takes is six ingredients to get there.

The dish starts with some onions and garlic sautéed in butter. These are then combined with cooked Italian sausage and cubed sweet potatoes. Everything is roasted together in a cast-iron skillet, showing how you can make this recipe with minimal effort and maximum tastiness.

Recipe: Sweet Potato and Sausage Hash.

In a recent development, there are never enough ways to use up those extra potatoes! This time, your floury potatoes like Yukon Golds or Russets take the lead with an herby potato galette. This particular recipe is a crustless galette, so there's no dough necessary, and you only need a handful of ingredients to make it.

In a recent development, to make the galette, shred the potatoes, add them to a hot skillet with lots of olive oil and sage, then press them down to help form a natural crust. Cook the potatoes for another 10 minutes as butter is added to the pan, then flip the whole thing and cook it on the other side. The result is a crispy potato pancake that's golden on the outside, soft on the inside, and delicious all the way around.

Recipe: Potato Galettes With Sage.

It's the ultimate Thanksgiving grilled cheese, so you don't want to pass this one up. You can make use of several leftover ingredients for this sandwich, both savory and sweet, such as extra apples and leftover ham.

In a recent development, apple butter is spread across two slices of sourdough bread, and then layered with Brie, diced ham, and diced apples before the sandwich is toasted in butter. This simply isn't your average grilled cheese sandwich; you also get bonus points if you can pair it with some butternut squash soup.

Recipe: Sweet and Savory Brie and Apple Butter Grilled Cheese.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wendy's is a beloved chain of fast food restaurants whose square-shaped burger patties are instantly recognizable to many American diners.
  • Sources indicate that the Sunshine State accounts for roughly 8% of the total number of locations this fast food giant has in the United States, compared to Texas, which has slightly fewer locations at 419.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy's is a beloved chain of fast food restaurants whose square-shaped burger patties are instantly recognizable to many American diners. Founded in 1969 in Columbus, Ohio, the brand is an institution where it was born — yet the Midwestern state doesn't actually have the most locations. Neither do populous hubs like California or New York. Rather, you need to look southeast to the land of orange groves. With 464 restaurants as of November 2026, Florida has more Wendy's locations than any other state in the country.

Sources indicate that the Sunshine State accounts for roughly 8% of the total number of locations this fast food giant has in the United States, compared to Texas, which has slightly fewer locations at 419. However, if you take population differences into account, there are more restaurants per capita in Florida than in the Lone Star State. This means that Florida residents are more likely to find a Wendy's nearby. Not everything seems to be bigger in Texas, after all, at least when it comes to this fast food chain.

Additionally, two Florida cities — Miami and Orlando — are in the top five U.S. cities with the most Wendy's locations (per ScrapeHero). So, whether you're enjoying the nightlife of South Beach or visiting Disney World, you won't be too far from a Jr. Bacon Cheeseburger. Despite Florida's distinction of having the most locations, however, it doesn't have the largest Wendy's in the world. That honor goes to Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, a country in the Caucasus region.

In a recent development, the idea of people vacationing in, moving to, or spending part of the year in Florida is an old trope, and there's a good reason for it. Many Americans see the state as a respite from the cold, and the Sunshine State actually has a long history of being a destination for migrants moving down from northern states, dating back to as early as the 1800s.

Interestingly, people from Ohio comprise a large portion of these migrants — in fact, according to USAFacts, more Ohioans moved to Florida than to any other state in 2024. Just like immigrants from other countries, American transplants bring their own cultures that can influence the local culinary scene, and maybe that's why there are so many Wendy's locations in the Sunshine State.

In a recent development, considering how the brand was founded in the Buckeye State, perhaps the many transplants brought their taste for the chain's iconic baked potatoes, chili, and square burgers with them. After all, Ohio has the third-largest number of Wendy's restaurants and has more locations per capita than Florida. It might seem like mere coincidence until you take into account the fact that Florida is also home to another Buckeye institution, Skyline Chili, and it's the only state outside the Midwest where the chain is present.

#46356. Tech Report: Crostata Di Mele (Italian Apple Pie) Recipe

Tech Report: Crostata Di Mele (Italian Apple Pie) Recipe

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer.
  • Recent findings suggest that my recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu.
  • Learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer. Although I tasted complex and ethereal cakes, pastries, and frozen delights, I kept coming back to the simple fruit crostatas: buttery crusts molded into tart pans or baked free-form in rustic rounds, topped with glistening fruits and cakey or custardy fillings. These desserts tasted like perfection in their simplicity and purity of flavors.

Recent findings suggest that my recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu. A traditional pasta frolla (Italian short dough) crust is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere (pastry cream custard) and topped with tart, crisp apples and crunchy turbinado sugar. The warm crostata is given a finishing glaze of melted apricot preserves, then chilled for serving.

Learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries. The dough is easy to work with, and the pastry cream is a versatile filling for other treats, such as profiteroles, layer cakes, or napoleons.

Sources indicate that there are 3 main components in the crostata di mele: the crust, the custard filling, and the toppings. For the crust, you will need all-purpose flour, granulated sugar, sea salt, cold unsalted butter, a large egg plus 1 yolk, vanilla extract, and the zest of a large lemon. The difference between this crostata dough and regular apple pie dough is the addition of eggs, which makes the dough slightly less flaky but more pliable for rolling and shaping. For the pastry cream, you will need whole milk, a vanilla bean, more lemon zest, 4 yolks, granulated sugar, and cornstarch. You will split the vanilla bean lengthwise to release the tiny black seeds into the milk, and the cornstarch acts as a thickening agent. To top the crostata, I like using apples that are crisp and tart, but that also have a balance of sweetness. Honeycrisp, Pink Lady, and Granny Smith are perfect apple varieties for this recipe. You will toss your apple slices with fresh lemon juice to prevent browning before baking, and use some melted butter to secure a crunchy sprinkling of turbinado sugar. To give your baked crostata a shiny finish, you will need apricot preserves to melt down and strain.

Combine the flour, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.

Add the butter a few pieces at a time and mix until pea-sized clumps form.

Add the egg, yolk, lemon zest, and vanilla, and mix until a dough forms.

Shape the dough into a disk, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes.

While the dough is chilling, heat the milk, vanilla bean, and lemon zest strips in a medium saucepan until it barely starts to simmer.

Remove the pan from the heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes.

Place a medium glass bowl on a damp kitchen towel or mat to prevent slipping.

Add the egg yolks, sugar, and cornstarch and whisk until thick and pale yellow.

Remove the vanilla bean and zest strips with a slotted spoon, then discard.

Gradually add the warm milk to the egg mixture, whisking constantly.

Sources indicate that transfer the mixture back to the saucepan and cook over low heat, stirring frequently until it comes to a boil. Turn the heat to low and whisk constantly for 1 minute.

Recent findings suggest that remove the pan from the heat, then scrape the filling into a heat-proof bowl and press a piece of plastic wrap to the surface. Chill for at least 2 hours.

In a large bowl, toss the apple slices with the lemon juice.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Press the dough into the pan and trim the excess flush with the edge of the pan.

Spread the cooled pastry cream evenly over the bottom of the pastry shell.

Arrange the slices in concentric overlapping circles over the pastry cream, starting from the outer edge and working inward.

Brush the apples with the melted butter and sprinkle on the turbinado sugar.

Bake the crostata di mele for about 50 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the apples are tender.

While the crostata is baking, heat the apricot jam with 1 tablespoon of water in a small saucepan until warm and liquid.

Strain the jam if any large pieces of fruit remain.

Remove the crostata from the oven and immediately brush on the apricot glaze.

Cool the crostata completely in the pan on a rack before removing from the pan.

Slice the crostata and serve at room temperature or chilled.

Our bakery-worthy crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere and topped with tart, crisp apples.

Sources indicate that the crostata is one of the most continuously made dessert forms found in Italian baking, dating back to the 1400s. Not only is the crostata found in pastry shops and on restaurant menus, but it is also the one dessert that many people make at home with whatever ingredients are on hand. This kind of humble tart was likely consumed at breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

It has been revealed that the crostata di mele probably originated in northern Italy, where apples are grown in abundance. In order to highlight the fresh flavor of the apples, crostata de mele is spiced with a light hand. Subtle cinnamon and a hint of nutmeg might be used, along with the zest of a lemon, as in this recipe. With only a few simple ingredients, the recipe is also dependent on using a light hand in preparation. The dough should be minimally handled to prevent a tough or shrunken crust. The pastry cream must be carefully tempered to prevent lumps from forming. And nothing should get in the way of the apples being the star.

Even though there may seem to be a lot of steps to this recipe, there are lots of ways to do advance prep to save time. First, your crostata dough can be mixed, shaped into a disk, wrapped, and chilled for several days in the refrigerator. You can also freeze this dough for up to 3 months. Once you are ready to roll out the dough, allow it to come to cool to room temperature before you shape it. You can also roll out and fill your tart pan, then wrap the unbaked shell and refrigerate or freeze until it is time to fill and bake.

Recent findings suggest that the pastry cream should only be made 1 or 2 days in advance, and this custardy filling should not be frozen unless it is layered into a dessert (too much separation will occur). Wait until just before baking to spread the pastry cream into your tart shell so that the dough will not become soggy.

From experience, I know that this crostata di mele will stay fresh, tasty, and sliceable for almost a week under refrigeration. That stated, it is crucial to always keep the crostata chilled to prevent bacterial growth in the custard layer. Typically, 3-5 days is the best range for serving this dessert.

Latest Update: 6 Best American Tex-Mex Chains, According To Customer Reviews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tex-Mex food is incredibly popular across the country, but the line between it and more traditional Mexican fare can be a bit hard to define.
  • Derived from Mexican and Tejano cooking methods, Tex-Mex was born out of a meeting of cultures that combined time-honored techniques and new ingredients.
  • Industry observers note that flour tortillas and dairy, like cheddar and Colby jack cheeses, are also major parts of the Tex-Mex food culture, as are queso dips and customizable combinations of rice, beans, proteins, and cheeses in a personal-sized bowl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tex-Mex food is incredibly popular across the country, but the line between it and more traditional Mexican fare can be a bit hard to define. Plus, there are other offshoots, like California or New Mexican styles that overlap with Tex-Mex but use different ingredients, such as avocados or hatch chiles. To cut down on some of the confusion, we've created this list to help you find the most reliable, tasty, and distinctly Tex-Mex quick service and casual restaurant chains you can dine at, according to the people who eat at them.

Derived from Mexican and Tejano cooking methods, Tex-Mex was born out of a meeting of cultures that combined time-honored techniques and new ingredients. For instance, cumin and dried chili powder had recently become available, and they swiftly caught on in Tex-Mex cooking. Now the pungent, earthy spices are heavily relied on for chili and stews.

Industry observers note that flour tortillas and dairy, like cheddar and Colby jack cheeses, are also major parts of the Tex-Mex food culture, as are queso dips and customizable combinations of rice, beans, proteins, and cheeses in a personal-sized bowl. Or you could just put all those elements together in an oversized burrito. Many of the restaurants on this list do just that, and all of them have been highly rated by fans for taste, price, and overall value. So, the next time you're craving fajitas, quesadillas, and refried beans, feel free to give one of these chains a visit to fulfill that hunger.

Founded in 1991, Mi Cocina is a beloved local chain with just over 20 locations throughout Texas, but the eatery's reputation stretches far further. The upscale Tex-Mex restaurant is just as known for its cocktails, especially the swirled Mambo Taxi Margarita, as it is for the food, such as the fajitas. The upscale brand's dishes include nachos al carbon, poblano chicken enchiladas, and pork picoso tamales that are so flavorful, you definitely won't want to put ketchup on them.

Customers rate the restaurant highly on user review platforms, with diners on Yelp saying things like, "Always consistently excellent! My go-to is the brisket tacos and a Dilemma Margarita!" Other guests agree, saying they always enjoy the food when they visit the chain. That reliability is one reason people are so quick to recommend the establishment. Even those who are quite particular about their Tex-Mex fall in love with the place, and many say they'll be back after their first time dining here.

Don't make the mistake of confusing Taco Cabana with Taco Bell. Both chains sell tacos, but the smaller restaurant still has a homemade feel, unlike the larger, Tex-Mex fast food super-seller. That's probably because Taco Cabana still makes its from-scratch food from fresh ingredients every day. The differences in flavor and feel in the restaurant's dishes are easy to identify, especially in the handmade flour tortillas. That helps ensure you'll never have to worry about one of the most notable elements of a satisfying burrito. And the ones here come overstuffed and covered in optional cheese sauce.

Diners here develop a passion for the chain, or as one TikTok commenter declared, "Taco Cabana is my FAVORITE fast food place. It beats Taco Bell hands down." It's not hard to see why someone might feel that way. Fans enjoy the restaurant's large portions, noting that nachos come in a box large enough to be mistaken for a pizza.

Sources indicate that the meats get their share of the limelight too, with customers recommending items like the beef and chicken fajita nachos, and the customizable protein bowl. One of the brand's latest hit items is the bean and cheese pie, a handheld psuedo-empanada filled with refried beans and yellow cheeses.

Uncle Julio's is an eatery that has understood the importance of making every dish from scratch since it opened several decades ago, and that includes the flour tortillas. The freshly made flatbread definitely tastes better than store-bought ones, which is why people can buy them by the dozen. And that's just one of the things that's made with care here. Dishes like guacamole that's made tableside and large burritos have led this Texas-based chain to expand into more than 30 locations.

People appreciate the restaurant's salsa, which holds a great middle-ground between mild and spicy, and praise the bacon-wrapped shrimp, which pairs juicy, seasoned seafood with crispy and chewy slices of pork. Others say they often have enough of their meal left to take some home, especially with dishes like the chicken and steak fajitas or the Tex-Mex combination dinner.

According to recent reports, this Tex-Mex establishment also has a unique dessert – interactive chocolate piñatas. Guests are encouraged to play with their food when the hanging ball of decorated chocolate is brought to the table. A few short taps later and the dessert cracks open to spill strawberries, churros, and other fruits onto the tray. It's another delicious and memorable way Uncle Julio's has found to fuse cultures before ending the evening.

Like several of the chains on this list, Fuzzy's Taco Shop was founded in Texas. But this one has gone on to become one of the largest of the homegrown brands, with more than 100 locations in 14 states. That growth was spurred forward by customers who enjoy the restaurant's sizable portions, flavors, and consistency on dishes ranging from breakfast burritos, quesadillas, nachos, and customizable bowls.

According to recent reports, first-time diners are impressed by the guacamole and overall experience of eating at Fuzzy's, and say they'll no doubt be returning soon. Others make it a point to visit the chain often, saying it's a great spot for birria tacos. In fact, one fan on Facebook called the dish "top notch," adding that the meal was perfectly made. Items like the grilled steak bowl and seasoned chips are so tasty they can even help people who normally eat at other Mexican-inspired places make the switch to Fuzzy's.

Sources indicate that guests are warmly greeted every time they walk through the doors at Moe's Southwest Grill, a tradition the business started at the first location in 2000. Since then, the tech giant has grown rapidly, now operating almost 550 stores across the nation. The brand is known for innovative flavors and good quality, and customers praise the queso, overstuffed burritos, and customizable bowls, which many say are better than other national brands.

It has been revealed that A TikTok user posted about their experience getting a nearly full bag of chips after ordering his mains, and that kind of generosity isn't rare at the chain. Another fan noted how stuffed the birria stack they ordered was, saying it was heavy to pick up, while a first-time diner was impressed by how large the bowl they ordered was.

Industry observers note that fans of Moe's have plenty of choices to customize their bowls and other meals with, but many find their favorite items and stick with them. That loyalty had one customer declaring a half-hour drive to the nearest store wasn't too far to go for the food, showing that not even a little distance can keep people away when a queso craving strikes. Or, as one Tripadvisor reviewer mentioned, "... food is splendid! All around just great establishment. We loved everything, especially the queso!!".

Recent findings suggest that the name Qdoba Mexican Eats might catch your attention, but it's the chain's food that keeps it. So much so that in the almost 30 years the restaurant has been open, Qdoba fans have formed a rivalry with those who prefer Chipotle, which just so happens to have also been founded in Denver in the 1990s. But Colorado residents prefer the smaller chain, with customers citing the brand's freshness, taste, and generosity with the queso keeps other national brands from comparing.

The establishment is known for the variety of fillings it offers, including steak and chicken that's grilled in-house. In addition to burrito bowls, you can customize a bowl of layered nachos, too. And the quesadillas can have some crunch added with a cheesy exterior crust. One Facebook user was so impressed by the restaurant that they posted, "I've been 5 times, the food is always fresh and hot [...] I've tried their quesadillas and bowl and I'm absolutely blown away every time with the quality. 10/10!".

Recent findings suggest that tex-Mex chains are popular and plentiful on the restaurant landscape, so narrowing down this list to the brands fans can't stop raving about took a bit of time. First, the criteria for how we'd be defining what makes a chain the best and what made it Tex-Mex were decided.

If the restaurants had a focus on flour tortillas, yellow cheeses, and cumin, alongside dishes, like nachos, enchiladas, fajitas, and queso, it qualified as a Tex-Mex establishment.

Industry observers note that the eateries had to have more than a dozen locations and good reviews for taste, value, and consistency across multiple sources. Those platforms included social media posts and comments, message boards, user review sites, and professional reviews. The final list was compiled after each chain's specific instances of customer satisfaction were tallied.

This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
  • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
  • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:.

“A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

The memory findings were more complicated.

Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

#46347. Add This Ingredient To French Toast For A Crispier Crust (Hint: It's Not Butter Or Oil)

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (615 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

Add This Ingredient To French Toast For A Crispier Crust (Hint: It's Not Butter Or Oil)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A classic French toast recipe is one of those comforting dishes that can be whipped up in a matter of minutes.
  • Semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is.
  • Recent findings suggest that just don't go overboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A classic French toast recipe is one of those comforting dishes that can be whipped up in a matter of minutes. However, one common problem people run into is soggy bread rather than a crisp, beautifully caramelized exterior. Unfortunately, sogginess is something of an occupational hazard when you're soaking bread in liquid. To give your slices more of a chance to thrive, all you need to do is add a little semolina flour to your soaking mixture. Two tablespoons per cup and a half of liquid is just about all you need.

Semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is. Compared to standard, powdery all-purpose flour, semolina is higher in protein and fiber, and its coarse grains are well-suited to soaking up moisture. In French toast, that can be the difference between a soggy exterior and a crispy one. A small amount turns a watery custard into a more structured batter that clings to the bread instead of letting it drink up all that liquid and fall apart before it even reaches the frying pan. Its subtle nuttiness also adds a whole newly introduced layer of complexity to the flavor of the French toast, and would pair wonderfully with some cosy nutmeg and cinnamon.

Recent findings suggest that just don't go overboard. Semolina is still flour, so balance is key. Add too little and the mixture stays watery; add too much, and you end up with something closer to a paste than a batter. We recommend starting with a small amount, around a tablespoon, then adjusting until you reach your desired consistency. Semolina flour takes time to absorb liquid, so once you've added it, let the custard sit for a minimum of 10 minutes before adding your bread. Once it's rested, it should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Sources indicate that semolina is one way to give French toast a crispy, lightly browned exterior, but it's by no means the only one. If you're having a hard time finding it, you can always swap in regular flour. The texture is different, but flour also absorbs liquid and thickens the batter, so you get largely the same effect, just without the nutty flavor. You could even skip the flour altogether and stir a cornstarch slurry into the custard, which packs even more thickening power. Just remember, as with semolina, moderation is key when adding flour or cornstarch into the mix.

Beyond thickening the custard, there are plenty of other handy tricks for shatteringly crispy French toast. To improve both its texture and flavor, give your bread a generous dusting of sugar after it comes out of the custard (before it hits the heat). Alton Brown might prefer honey over sugar in his French toast, but we'd argue that's a rare mistake. See, once sugar hits the heat, it starts to caramelize, melting into a crisp, brûléed crust and infusing the bread with a rich, toasty flavor. Keep the heat moderate, since caramelization can quickly turn to burning without proper care.

If you're not sold on the idea of messing around with the batter or adding extra ingredients, you can guarantee crispy French toast from the get-go by using stale bread. This might not sound too appetizing, but hear us out. Bread that's around one to two days old has lost a good chunk of its moisture, which leaves it firmer and drier. It acts like a sponge, soaking up the custard without turning to mush, so you get a rich, eggy center and a browned exterior instead of a soggy, limp slice.

Chili is one of those meals that scratches an itch that no other comfort food can quite compare to. You can go with beans or no beans, or even make a super satisfying vegan version. A major batch can be pretty easy to make in the slow cooker, but despite the simple prep, it still takes a lot of time. So, when you want a quick hit, you can always reach for your favorite brand of the canned stuff. However, there's an easy trick to up the flavor of your meal — add a dash of instant coffee. The incredible blend of flavors might just blow your mind.

It has been revealed that instant coffee crystals will add some bold, roasted richness to your chili. Sure, coffee is bitter, but if you don't go overboard, its presence will be subtle, making your chili taste more like something homemade that's been simmering on the stove all day. It creates a nice depth by enhancing the perception of the beefy umami and highlighting spices like cumin, coriander, cayenne, and chili powder. It can also help offset some of the perceived acidity in the tomato-heavy sauce, giving you an end result that's more balanced on the palate and beautifully tied together.

Sources indicate that if you don't already have instant coffee in the pantry, instant espresso, like Medaglia D'Oro Instant Espresso, is sometimes preferred because it dissolves more easily, but really, any instant coffee will work. Just keep in mind that espresso will have a stronger flavor, and the strength of any given coffee crystals can vary a bit. Start with just a pinch, or about a ¼ teaspoon per 15-ounce can of chili. You can dissolve it in a few spoonfuls of hot water first to ensure it doesn't clump, but if the chili is already simmering, it should blend in easily, especially in small amounts. Give it a taste and add more if you'd like.

It has been revealed that if you want to go for bolder undertones, a touch of cocoa powder pairs nicely with coffee crystals. If you want to skip the instant coffee and use the real thing, you can add a little brewed coffee or finely ground espresso (but when using the latter, you'll need to mix it into a paste with some water so you don't end up with a mouthful of grounds). A splash of bourbon, or even beer, can help round out the flavor with the coffee. And much like it works in chili, instant coffee can wake up your spaghetti sauce. But to get that great earthy, bold flavor in a full meal right off the shelf, you're going to want to try coffee crystals in your canned chili.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?

Recent findings suggest that many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question. It’s almost like they’re professionally trained in the art of dodging conversation.

Industry observers note that the thing is, kids actually do want to talk. You just have to ask the right questions: ones that spark their imagination, make them laugh, or invite them to share something meaningful on their terms.

Industry observers note that so, meet them where they are. Instead of the same old, “How was your day?” (which, let’s be honest, will never yield a thrilling response), try questions that make them pause and think for a moment. This way, you’re not prying information out of them, you’re building a habit of open conversation, one fun question at a time.

Ask them in the car, at bedtime, over breakfast, or whenever your kid is in a chatty mood. You might be surprised at what they share — and the hilarious, heartwarming, or even unexpectedly deep conversations that follow.

Sources indicate that laughter is one of the easiest ways to connect with your child (and can boost your mental health too). These offbeat, ridiculous questions will get them giggling while giving you a glimpse into their wonderfully weird little minds.

Would you rather have a banana for a nose or popcorn for ears? Kids love absurd choices, and these “would you rather” questions are a surefire way to spark hilarious debates.

Would you rather have spaghetti for hair or marshmallows for fingers?

Would you rather live in a house made of chocolate or a castle made of cheese?

Would you rather always talk in rhymes or only be able to whisper?

Would you rather ride a roller coaster that never ends or a Ferris wheel that goes super fast?

Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?

Ever wonder what your backpack thinks about your daily routine? These questions help kids think outside the box — and maybe appreciate their favorite objects a little more.

If your backpack could complain, what would it say?

Sources indicate that what if the moon really was made of cheese? These questions let kids build wild, imaginary worlds where anything is possible.

If you could invent a upcoming holiday, what would it be called and how would we celebrate?

If you could make one silly law that everyone had to follow, what would it be?

What do you wish clouds were made of?

If you had a magic remote that could pause or rewind real life, when would you use it?

What’s better than food? Food-related nonsense! These questions are perfect for mealtime giggles.

What’s the silliest pizza topping combination you can think of?

Forget the usual “What’s your favorite color?” These questions dig a little deeper into what makes your child them — their dreams, their interests, and how they see the world.

Who are they, really? These questions help kids define what makes them special. Who knows? They might even surprise themselves with their answers.

If you could rename yourself, what would you want to be called?

What’s something you’re really good at?

What’s one thing that makes you feel really proud of yourself?

Recent findings suggest that every kid has dreams. These questions encourage them to think big.

If you could have any job in the world when you grow up, what would it be?

If you could live anywhere in the world, where would it be?

If you could suddenly have super-skill, what would it be?

If you could invent something to make life easier, what would it do?

What’s something you dream about doing one day?

What’s school really like? What do they wish adults understood? These questions help you see the world through their eyes.

If you could be principal of your school for a day, what rules would you change?

What’s one thing about school you wish was different?

Forget the usual “favorite color” and “favorite food” questions — these favorites are a little more unexpected.
