These questions help kids think outside the box and explore upcoming ideas — without it feeling like homework.

Sources indicate that what if everything was upside down? What if people lived in the ocean? These questions let kids stretch their creativity and invent a world of their own.

If you could switch lives with any fictional character, who would it be?

If you could time travel, would you rather visit the past or the future?

If you could build a brand-new planet, what would it be like?

If you could talk to any historical figure, who would you pick and what would you ask?

If you could live in any book or movie world, which one would you choose?

Industry observers note that kids love hypotheticals, especially ridiculous ones. These questions tap into their curiosity and creativity.

If aliens landed in our backyard, what would be the first thing you’d say to them?

If you could talk to animals, what’s the first thing you’d ask them?

If you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

If you could be invisible for a day, what would you do?

If you could wake up with a superpower, which one would you want?

Kids are natural philosophers. Sometimes, they just need the right question to get them going.

What’s something you’ve always been curious about but never asked?

If you could solve one big mystery in the world, what would it be?

If you could design your dream school, what classes would you add?

What’s something that happens in nature that seems magical to you?

What do you think is the coolest invention ever made?

These questions encourage kids to see things in a newly introduced way, whether it’s about themselves, the world, or the future.

What’s something small that can make a significant difference?

What’s a time when you changed your mind about something?

If you could ask the president one question, what would it be?

What’s one way kids can change the world?

What’s something you wish you knew how to do?

In a recent development, kids may not always have the words to explain their feelings, but these thoughtful questions help create a safe space for them to share what’s in their hearts. The Feelings Wheel can be a good visual aid for this too.

Industry observers note that sometimes, kids just need the right words to talk about how they feel. These questions give them a way to open up.

What’s something that made you feel really happy this week?

What’s a time when you felt really proud of yourself?

What’s something that always makes you feel loved?

What’s a time when you felt really brave?

What’s something you wish people knew about you?

It’s not always easy to talk about the hard stuff, but these questions can help kids express their feelings in a safe way.

What’s something that helps you feel better when you’re sad?

What’s a time when something felt really hard, but you got through it?

What’s one thing that makes you feel nervous?

What’s something you do when you’re feeling frustrated?

Friends are a huge part of kids’ lives — these questions help them reflect on what friendship means to them.

What do your friends do to make you feel special?

What’s something you love doing with your family?

If you could plan the perfect day with your best friend, what would you do?

Slowing down and noticing the good things is a skill kids can carry with them for life. These questions make space for reflection.

What’s something you’re really grateful for today?

What’s a small thing that makes a big difference in your day?

What’s a memory that always makes you smile?

What’s something you love about yourself?

What’s one thing you want to remember about being a kid when you’re older?

These questions are designed to spark deeper connections and create shared experiences — because the best conversations are about connecting.

Every family has inside jokes, traditions, and funny moments. These questions bring them to the surface.

What’s your favorite family tradition?

If you could plan a dream family vacation, where would we go?

What’s something funny that has happened in our family?

What’s a meal we should cook together soon?

If we could create a secret family handshake, what would it look like?

Remember that time we all got soaked in the rain? Or the time you laughed so hard you snorted? These questions help relive the best moments.

What’s the best day you’ve ever had?

What’s something we’ve done together that made you laugh really hard?

What’s the silliest story I’ve ever told you?

What’s one thing we should do more often as a family?

What’s next for our family? These questions invite kids to dream up exciting adventures — real or imagined.

If we could go on a wild adventure tomorrow, what would we do?

What’s a hobby or activity you’d love for us to try together?

If you could design the perfect family game night, what would we play?

If we could time travel together, what era would we visit?

If we started a family business, what would we sell?

Every family has its own kind of magic. These questions bring it out in unexpected ways.

If our family had a theme song, what would it be?

If we could invent a latest family tradition, what would it be?

If you could give everyone in our family a superpower, what would they be?

If every member of our family was an animal, what would it be?

What’s a way we can make someone else’s day better together?

What’s one thing you want me to always remember about you?

💙 Mel Mah’s Kids Bedtime Routine can help you all wind down in a peaceful way, together.

The best questions to ask kids are open-ended, playful, and relevant to their world. Instead of asking, “Did you have a good day?”—which almost always leads to a dead-end answer—try something that sparks their imagination or invites storytelling, like “What was the funniest thing that happened today?” or “If you could switch places with your teacher for a day, what would you do?” Kids are much more likely to engage when a question feels fun, unexpected, and free of pressure.

Kids love absurdity, so the weirder and wackier the question, the better. Offbeat questions tap into their creativity, making conversation feel more like a game than a chore.

Sources indicate that silly questions are also a great way to bond, especially when you play along. If your kid tells you they’d rather ride a roller coaster that never stops over a Ferris wheel that goes super fast, ask why and join in the fun by sharing your own ridiculous answer.

Laughter is a powerful connector, and sometimes the most unexpected conversations start with a totally goofy question.

For 6-year-olds, short questions about things they can picture work best. Silly choices and pretend play go over well. Try “What would you name a pet cloud?” or “If your stuffed animals had jobs, what would they be?” Many of the funny questions above fit this age, especially the “would you rather” and “If your stuff could talk” lists. Ask one question at a time, since young kids can lose the thread when you ask two at once.

Which question to ask depends on what you want from the chat. If you want laughs, pick a “would you rather” or other funny question. If you want to know your child better, choose from the get-to-know list. For big feelings, try the emotional expression questions. When you’re not sure, start silly to help them relax, then move to a deeper one.

Kids spend a lot of their day being told what to do—sit still, follow directions, finish their homework—so having a space where they get to lead the conversation is powerful. Asking fun and engaging questions gives them a chance to express themselves, think creatively, and feel heard without any right or wrong answers. It also helps build communication skills, emotional intelligence, and a sense of connection with you.

Beyond that, these questions create opportunities for everyday bonding. A quick chat in the car or during dinner can turn into a meaningful moment of connection. The more kids feel like their thoughts and ideas are valued, the more likely they are to open up — not just about the silly stuff but about the big things, too.

The key to getting good answers is making the conversation feel natural, not forced. If you ask a question and get a one-word response, don’t panic — sometimes kids just need a little extra space to warm up. Try following up with, “Tell me more!” or sharing your own answer first to get the ball rolling. If they see that you’re genuinely interested (and willing to be a little silly yourself), they’ll be more likely to engage.

Also, be thoughtful about your timing. Some kids open up more when they’re relaxed—like at bedtime or when you’re doing an activity together—while others chat more when they’re distracted, like in the car. If they’re tired, hungry, or mid-screen time, you might not get much out of them. But if you catch them in the right moment, you might just unlock a goldmine of thoughts, ideas, and hilarious kid logic.

Sources indicate that the best time to ask kids questions is when they’re naturally more open to conversation — when they feel safe, relaxed, and not pressured to respond. For some kids, that’s during bedtime, when they’re winding down and their thoughts start to flow. For others, it’s in the car, when there’s no pressure for eye contact and they can talk freely. Meal times, walks, or even while playing with Legos can also be great moments to slip in a fun question.

It has been revealed that trying to force deep conversation right after school when their brain is fried or when they’re engrossed in a game or show usually won’t work. Instead, look for organic, low-pressure moments when chatting feels easy. And remember, it’s not about when you ask, it’s about showing up consistently so that when they are ready to talk, they know you’ll be there to listen.

#46341. What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.
  • Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?
  • ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

In a recent development, in perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

In a recent development, however, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

Okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and indicates, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”.

I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

[Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?].

Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

Recent findings suggest that there is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

Q: Does ADHD get worse as you get older?

Sources indicate that ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

Recent findings suggest that david W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at first glance, tuna salad may appear to be a fairly set-in-stone formula. You mix the tinned fish with mayo, add in some aromatics, and enjoy the dish on bread or standalone. Yet start trialing creative add-ins, and tuna salad welcomes a surprisingly wide array of ingredients. There are so many ways to take plain tuna salad to the next level. A sharp cheddar cheese is one unexpected flavor boost.

After all, creaminess is a central part of the dish's appeal. And as a dairy product, cheddar cheese offers such a smooth mouthfeel in spades. However, unlike a simple mayo dressing, the cheese comes with a punch. Aging develops complex flavors, which can vary from barely perceptible tartness to rich nuttiness to a bold bite. Usually, the older the cheddar, the more amplified the flavor — although as the cheese develops, it loses some creaminess to become crumbly.

Sources indicate that for a top-tier cheddar tuna salad, go with a balanced option, aged for around six to nine months. Usually classified specifically as sharp, such a cheese is right when the acidic flavors turn into a bold bite — perfect for a tuna salad. So cube up the cheese, using two ounces per can of tuna, then stir everything up with some salt, onions, celery, and your other go-to tuna salad fold-ins. You'll get a dish that's still comforting, but also comes with revamped flair.

It has been revealed that as America's favorite cheese, cheddar certainly belongs in a dish like tuna salad. While it's not common to mix cheese directly into the salad, the inclusion is reminiscent of a beloved tuna salad application: a tuna melt. Originating by mistake, the tuna melt proves that fish and cheese do belong on the same plate, especially if tuna's involved.

Further embrace the two dishes by heating the cheddar cheese tuna salad. The cheese will turn molten inside — not only on top — of the fish, making for an extra-satisfying filling. Pair that with a nice bread, say a classic American white loaf, a deli-inspired rye, or a dependable sourdough, and you've got a terrific sandwich on your hands.

Sources indicate that not to say there's not more magic to explore with a cold cheddar tuna salad, too. The cheesy rendition is a befitting tuna pasta salad twist. Or balance out cheddar's richness by rolling the salad into lettuce wraps, a delicious appetizer option. Cheddar gives tuna salad that extra oomph, turning the basic dish into a centerpiece meal.

#46337. Breaking: Empathy vs compassion: the difference (with real-life examples)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Empathy vs compassion: the difference (with real-life examples)

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships.
  • Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.
  • Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Sources indicate that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships. Whether it’s a friend going through a tough time or a family member facing a challenge, how we connect with them can significantly impact the support we offer.

Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.

Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering. Compassion isn’t just a fleeting emotion — it’s a lasting state, a readiness to extend a helping hand whenever possible. (For the full definition, here’s our guide to what compassion is.).

Empathy is the capability to tune into someone else’s emotions and to feel what they’re feeling. Empathy means genuinely trying to understand another person’s feelings and perspective.

💙 Sharpen your listening skills and make others truly feel heard with Jay Shetty in this Supportive Listening meditation.

While both empathy and compassion are avenues to connect with others, their core essence and impact are different. While empathy allows for emotional understanding, compassion takes it further by driving action. It's about moving from feeling to doing, from emotional resonance to proactive kindness.

Through this understanding, we can see the value of cultivating empathy and practicing compassion in our daily actions, which not only enrich our relationships but positively impact our communities, too.

Empathy steers emotional connection. It's about feeling the same emotions that another person is experiencing and aligning emotionally because of that similarity. On the other hand, compassion drives us towards a deep understanding of another's distress, coupled with a desire to make them feel better. It's not just about feeling, it’s about understanding and taking action.

Empathy is rooted in deeply feeling what another person is going through and mirroring their emotional state. Compassion is about acknowledging what the other people are going through instead of feeling the emotion yourself.

Empathy often revolves around an inward reflection that allows us to feel the emotions that another person is experiencing. Compassion propels us outward and encourages acting on the feeling to help alleviate someone else’s discomfort.

Empathy primarily consists of feeling the emotional state of another, while compassion is action-oriented. Compassion prompts us to take steps to ease another's suffering, no matter how small.

Industry observers note that empathy, although a profound feeling, can be more of a momentary emotional connection that is often fleeting once the shared emotion dissipates. Compassion, on the other hand, reflects a long-term commitment to assisting others and a consistent readiness to help.

In a recent development, 💙 Learn more about Empathy vs. Compassion with this Daily Jay session.

Industry observers note that you usually won’t choose between them in the moment. They tend to show up together. Here’s how each one can look in the same situation.

Empathy is feeling with someone. Compassion is taking a step to help. You won’t usually pick one in the moment, since feeling with someone is often what leads you to help.

Empathy and compassion are ways to connect with others, but they play different roles. Empathy is about feeling the same emotions that someone else is feeling. For example, if a friend is sad, you feel sad along with them. Compassion takes empathy a step further. It’s about recognizing someone’s distress and wanting to help alleviate it. So, when you see someone in trouble, not only do you understand their problem, but you also want to help sort it out. Compassion motivates us to act and make a positive difference, while empathy encourages us to feel and relate.

Sources indicate that both empathy and compassion are valuable in building meaningful relationships. Empathy helps in understanding other people’s emotions and creating bonds. Compassion, however, not only understands but also propels us to take action to help. It’s about moving from feeling to doing something helpful. Empathy can be a stepping stone to compassion, leading us from feeling to taking positive action.

Sources indicate that being empathetic and compassionate is like having a superpower for creating solid and supportive relationships. Empathy allows you to understand others' feelings, while compassion motivates you to take action to help. It’s a blend that encourages understanding while making a positive impact in others’ lives. Empathy and compassion go hand in hand, enhancing our connections with others and making our social interactions more meaningful and enriching.

Sources indicate that empathetic and compassionate leadership both aim to create a supportive work environment, but they do so in slightly different ways. Empathetic leadership is about understanding employees' emotions and perspectives and creating an environment where people feel heard and understood. Compassionate leadership, on the other hand, not only understands but takes action to support and help employees, recognizing the challenges and actively working to provide support or solutions. Compassionate leadership often brings a more supportive and caring work culture, benefiting both employees and the organization.

Q: “My Spouse Complains About My ADHD Constantly!”

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.
  • Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.
  • First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Sources indicate that let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

According to recent reports, this sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

According to recent reports, finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
  • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
  • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially vital at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, noted:.

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

#46332. World Kindness Day 2026: what it is and 7 ways to join in

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1391 w)

World Kindness Day 2026: what it is and 7 ways to join in

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined.
  • Moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about.
  • Read on for the story behind the day, what the research says about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

The barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined. You lean over, tap your phone, and cover the $4. They turn around, flustered, and thank you twice. The line keeps moving, but your morning feels a bit lighter.

Moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about. Every year on November 13, it celebrates how acts of goodwill can brighten an ordinary day, for those receiving and performing them.

Read on for the story behind the day, what the research says about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.

World Kindness Day is an unofficial global observance that encourages acts of kindness, massive and small. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 13. The day was first observed in 1998 and grew out of the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations rather than a single founder.

According to recent reports, the coalition formed at a conference in Tokyo, and it included founding members from Japan, Singapore, Australia, Canada, Thailand, the U.K., and the U.S. They chose November 13 because it was the conference’s opening day and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement. Today, classrooms, offices, and communities around the world honor the day.

You’ve probably felt it: you do something kind and your mood instantly lifts. Researchers have studied this effect, and here’s what they’ve found.

Industry observers note that in a 2023 study from The Ohio State University, 122 adults with moderate to severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assigned to one of three activities for several weeks. They either did acts of kindness, planned social activities, or practiced cognitive reappraisal, which means looking at a stressful event from a newly introduced angle.

Recent findings suggest that all three activities helped, but kindness did more than cognitive reappraisal to ease depression and anxiety. The kindness group was also the only one that reported feeling more connected to others.

Other research points the same way. A review of 27 studies covering more than 4,000 people indicated that performing acts of kindness gave people a modest but noticeable boost in their well-being.

Kindness may also lighten a hard day. In a two-week diary study of 77 adults, people tracked their stress, their mood, and how they helped others each day. Stress usually dragged positive emotion down, but on high-stress days when people helped more than usual, their mood held steady. In other words, a little extra kindness seemed to cushion the blow of a stressful day.

A note on the research: Most of this research is short-term and relies on self-reported mood, so we can’t say how long the benefits last. Kindness can support your well-being, but it doesn’t replace professional care. If anxiety, low mood, or stress lasts for weeks, it’s worth talking to a doctor.

Sources indicate that you don’t need a grand gesture. These seven ideas fit into a regular day, whether you’re at home, at work, or anywhere in between. You can also adjust any of them to fit your time, energy, and budget.

There’s probably someone on your mind — a friend you know is having a hard time, a relative you haven’t caught up with lately, or an old coworker you miss.

Sources indicate that mention the moment you thought of them, like “Saw a dog that looked like yours and had to say hi. Hope you’re doing okay.” Add “no need to reply” at the end, in case they’re feeling down or overwhelmed and might not have the energy for a back-and-forth.

💙 Before you send your message, read our guide to loving-kindness meditation.

According to recent reports, leave a short review for a small business, or send a note to a service worker who made your day. Write what you appreciated, such as the waiter who kept checking on your table or the mechanic who explained the repair without talking down to you.

For a coworker, send a note to their manager, who may not otherwise hear about their good work.

💙 Reflect on who you want to thank with the 7 Days of Gratitude course on Calm.

A quick “love your shoes” is nice, but a more specific compliment reveals someone that you’re really paying attention, and that you care. Praise someone for how patient they were with a difficult customer or how useful their point was in the meeting.

It takes only a few seconds, but noticing the details can mean more to someone than you might expect.

💙 Sharpen your compliments with Jay Shetty’s Effective Praise session on Calm.

Look for small things that would make someone’s day better and take care of one: carry the heavy bag, refill the empty printer, or take on the household chore nobody wants to do.

When you spot a need early, you can spare someone the awkwardness of asking.

💙 Keep the kindness moving with Jay Shetty’s Pay It Forward session on Calm.

Recent findings suggest that buy lunch for your colleague, round up a tip, or add a friend’s drink to your order. Set an amount before you head out, so a kind impulse doesn’t turn into a money worry later.

If your budget is a concern, the next idea includes free ways to help.

Many organizations also offer remote tasks, like writing cards or tutoring online.

💙 Start close to home with Jay Shetty’s Community Service session on Calm.

Recent findings suggest that kindness toward yourself counts, and it’s often overlooked. Notice how you talk to yourself when something goes wrong, then ask whether you’d say it that way to a friend. If you wouldn’t, here’s a quick way to try a kinder tone.

Try: A short self-compassion pause. Place a hand on your chest, take one slow breath, and name how you feel (“this is a lot right now”). Then say what you’d tell a friend in the same situation (“that sounds hard”).

💙 Press play on Calm’s Friend on the Inside meditation with Jeff Warren.

The World Kindness Movement created the day to encourage kind acts around the world. For many people, it’s also an invitation to do the kind thing they’ve been putting off, like thanking a neighbor.

World Kindness Day in 2026 is on Friday, November 13. It falls on November 13 every year, so only the day of the week changes.

World Kindness Day is on November 13 because it was the opening day of the first World Kindness Movement conference in Tokyo, and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement.

No single person started World Kindness Day. The World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations from seven countries, released the day in Tokyo.

Sources indicate that no, World Kindness Day and Random Acts of Kindness Day are two separate observances. World Kindness Day is November 13, while Random Acts of Kindness Day is February 17. They share the same spirit, so you’re welcome to celebrate both.

Studies suggest kindness can be good for you. Acts of kindness have been linked to better mood, lower anxiety, and stronger connection with others.

Recent findings suggest that in one diary study, stressful days usually made people feel less happy and upbeat. But on days when people helped others more than usual, that drop in positive feelings was smaller.

Sources indicate that kindness supports well-being, but it doesn’t replace care. Speak to a doctor if anxiety, stress, or low mood lasts for weeks.

💙 Here’s how you can lower your stress naturally.

If you’re feeling drained, it’s okay to start with yourself. A kind word to yourself counts, and some days it’s all you have energy for. When you have more to give, something small and thoughtful is plenty, like holding the door for someone or letting someone go ahead of you in line.

There’s no official color for World Kindness Day, so you can wear whatever feels good. Some schools and groups pick a color for their own events.

Q: “Are My Child’s Tummy Aches a Sign of Stress?”

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.
  • Sources indicate that Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches.
  • As parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Sources indicate that Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”.

As parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

Industry observers note that understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

According to recent reports, observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

It has been revealed that are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

It has been revealed that keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”].

And remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

Liz Nissim, Ph.D., is a clinical and school psychologist specializing in parenting and executive function coaching for neurodivergent children and teens.

#46322. AI anxiety: 5 ways to cope when you’re scared of AI

AI anxiety: 5 ways to cope when you’re scared of AI

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone.
  • AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing.
  • AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone. Chief Clinical Officer at Calm, Chris Mosunic, PhD, has tips and strategies to help tame a growing source of anxiety.

AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing. It isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but the feelings are real and common. They can focus on everyday risks, such as job loss and AI-powered scams, and bigger ones, such as AI getting out of human control.

AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools. A 2023 Calm survey* found that nearly 1 in 3 U.S. adults (29%) felt anxious about AI, and 18% described their feelings as fear or dread. At the same time, 31% felt optimistic, and 31% felt excited. Many respondents felt a mix: amazed by AI and nervous about it.

According to recent reports, concern about AI has stayed high in the years since. In a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey, 52% of U.S. adults mentioned they feel more concerned than excited about AI in daily life. That’s up from 37% in 2021 and about the same as in 2023. Just 9% said they feel more excited than concerned.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to know how AI will affect our safety and our lives. You might wonder how it will change your job, what it could mean for areas like scientific research, and what the future will look like. Many of us find uncertainty hard to cope with, so feeling anxious or out of control is understandable. But when anxiety feels overwhelming, it can start to affect your sleep, mood, and focus.

These five ways to manage AI anxiety draw on mindfulness and common thinking traps, like catastrophizing. Start with whichever fits how you feel today.

The rapid rise in AI and automation can feel like a threat to our livelihoods (and even our lives), making many of us feel unstable and out of control.

Resist resisting: When confronted with uncertainty, our first instinct can often be to fight it. Try sitting with it instead. Notice how the discomfort shows up in your body and mind.

Go at your own pace: Give yourself time to adjust to the new realities of AI.

Talk it out: Process your anxieties with a friend or a coworker. You may find someone who feels the same way.

💙 On those days when you feel overwhelmed by the rapidly changing tech landscape, try a simple meditation practice like Pause to Breathe to help you feel more grounded.

Industry observers note that if you’re feeling anxious or uneasy about AI, don’t invalidate or try to avoid those emotions — that approach can make things worse. Instead, let yourself feel anxious. Telling yourself you’re overreacting can damage your self-trust and self-confidence.

Identify the emotions: Get a better understanding of what you’re feeling. Your anxiety could mean you’re working through a more deeply rooted problem, like feeling threatened or inadequate.

Try meditation: Meditation can help you ground yourself in the present moment and tune into what you’re feeling and where it’s coming from.

Write down all your anxieties without censoring yourself: Set aside dedicated time each day to think through your anxious thoughts, helping you process and make sense of your emotions.

💙 Take some time to stop and do this short Emotions Check-In to make space for any anxious feelings.

When we’re feeling anxious about the unknown, many of us fall into the trap of catastrophic thinking, imagining the worst possible outcome, even without evidence to support it. This can cause low-level anxieties to spiral out of control.

Challenge your worst fears: What evidence do you have that they’re true or that they’ll happen?

Industry observers note that bring to mind times in the past that felt groundbreaking in the tech world: Think back to the creation of mobile phones, laptops, or even navigation apps, and consider how you’ve adapted to their existence despite any initial anxieties or concerns. The same could happen with AI.

Bring your mind back to the now: The future feels a whole lot less intimidating when you focus on the present.

💙 One of the best ways you can bring yourself back to the present is through mindfulness meditation, which you can learn in the Mindfulness for Beginners series.

It has been revealed that many of us find ourselves viewing situations as an all-or-nothing approach. This is a cognitive distortion called polarized thinking, and it often occurs because we’re focused on the extremes without considering the nuances or possibilities of any given situation.

The debate around AI is nuanced. Popular culture highlights dystopian futures, so it can be easy to think there’s only one possible outcome with AI.

In a recent development, however, reality tends to exist in between the extremes, so remind yourself that it’s perfectly normal for opposing emotions or views to be present at the same time. And they can also all feel as strong, real, or true as each other. You can feel fascinated and terrified, anxious and excited, or resentful and grateful.

In a recent development, when we allow multiple truths to co-exist in our minds, we make space for more ease. So try to hold space for the contradictions and the possibilities.

💙 For a more in-depth discussion on how to use mindfulness to combat worrying and keep nuance at the forefront, check out the Overcome Stress & Anxiety series.

At the extreme end of AI anxiety, some of us may have a deep—even subconscious—fear about a machine taking over. We ask questions like: Is this the beginning of the end of humanity? Will humans be replaced by robots?

Sources indicate that A fear of overdependence on technology can cause us to worry about the negative consequences of relying too heavily on artificial intelligence. One way to remedy this fear is to embrace our humanity.

Be present for the little things you often take for granted, like hugs, laughing until it hurts, or exchanging a look with your best friend.

Make time for the people in your life, and prioritize connecting with them face-to-face when you can.

Marvel at the awesomeness of human things like awkward silences or goosebumps when you’re listening to music.

Ask people how they’re really feeling and practice deep listening when they respond.

Disconnect from technology and spend time in nature.

💙 Embrace the power of being human and living in the now by reading a book, listening to a meditation, or taking a Mindful Walk.

*Calm research was fielded among n = 450 adults in the US between March 21, 2023 and March 22, 2023 and is nationally representative, with quotas across age, gender, race, ethnicity, and region.

Industry observers note that recent news stories have shown how general-purpose AI tools may respond in unsafe or harmful ways, especially when people are vulnerable or struggling with a mental health crisis. These situations are rare, but they highlight an important truth: AI is not human and can’t accurately recognize risk, provide crisis support, or understand the complexity of your emotional world.

AI can support mental health — especially when it’s part of a program designed and guided by licensed professionals. But general AI tools, like chatbots or large language models, are not a replacement for real human care.

If you’re struggling, please consider reaching out to a therapist or support line — many offer free or low-cost options. You deserve support that’s personal, thoughtful, and real.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. - Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Worldwide - Visit findahelpline.com for free, confidential resources.

Your mental health matters and you don’t have to navigate tough moments alone.

To manage anxiety about artificial intelligence, there are proactive steps you can take.

Educate yourself about AI to understand its capabilities and limitations better: Learning about AI can make it feel less intimidating.

Engage in conversations about AI: Talking with others about your concerns can offer new perspectives and reduce feelings of isolation.

Practice mindfulness and stress-reduction techniques: Managing your anxiety effectively can help you focus on the present and reduce worries about the future.

Stay informed about AI developments: Understand how it's being integrated into society to help you feel more prepared and less anxious.

Sources indicate that fear of artificial intelligence is common and can stem from several concerns, such as uncertainty about how AI will affect the future, including potential changes in the job market and societal norms. You may also have concerns about privacy, security, and the ethical use of AI. The idea of losing control to machines or facing decisions made by algorithms without empathy can be daunting.

Understanding these fears and addressing them through education and dialogue can help alleviate the anxiety associated with AI.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to be, though some concern is understandable. AI is changing fast, and it raises real questions, from job loss and scams to whether people can keep control of it. Some risks deserve attention. Others are far from certain, and no one knows exactly how AI will unfold. When we’re anxious, our minds jump to the worst outcome and can treat every headline as proof of a disastrous future.

It has been revealed that it can help to follow reliable news sources and take breaks from stories that leave you on edge. When your thoughts race ahead, try a mindfulness practice to bring your attention back to today. If worry about AI is getting in the way of sleep or daily life, consider talking with a therapist or doctor.

The fear of AI doesn’t have a widely recognized specific term but is often considered a form of “technophobia,” which is the fear of advanced technology or complex devices. When this fear centers on AI, it can stem from concerns that the technology could surpass human intelligence and from the ethical consequences of machines making decisions that affect people’s lives. AI anxiety is rooted in the unknown future impact of AI on humanity.

While AI offers many benefits, concerns about its negative effects remain. These include potential job losses due to automation, as AI can perform some tasks more efficiently than humans. Privacy issues are also a significant concern, as AI systems can process vast amounts of personal data, sometimes without clear consent or transparency. Security risks may arise if AI systems are hacked or malfunction. AI can also perpetuate bias if its training data is biased, leading to unfair or unethical decisions.

On a societal level, increased reliance on AI could reduce human interaction and erode certain skills as machines take over more tasks. Understanding these potential negative effects can help develop strategies to mitigate them and ensure AI is used responsibly and ethically.

Sources indicate that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

Spike in ADHD, Autism Diagnoses Driven by Broader Recognition, Understanding

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two new studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.
  • ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two latest studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two new studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.

ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two latest studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

It has been revealed that the first study, published in JAMA Psychiatry,2 evaluated the health records of 71,000 children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and 713,000 controls; it found that the annual number of individuals in the nationwide Danish health registry with newly diagnosed ADHD and/or ASD increased from 4,944 in 2012 to 9,179 in 2022. The proportion of girls diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and the median age at diagnosis also grew during the 10-year study period from 2012 to 2022.

However, traditional risk factors strongly linked to an ADHD or ASD diagnosis in 2012, such as low birth weight or lower household income, have become progressively less predictive with time. For example, children born with a low birth weight were 54% more likely to receive a subsequent diagnosis of ADHD or ASD in 2012; by 2022, that percentage dropped to 17%. Overall, the study found that children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD today more closely resemble their neurotypical peers compared to those diagnosed 10 years ago.

These findings do not mean that ADHD or ASD has become less impairing; the spectrum of cases has shifted as clinicians get better at identifying less obvious cases. Greater awareness of ADHD and ASD, and broader access to diagnostic assessment tools, are also factors contributing to growing diagnoses among children.

It has been revealed that “The study results do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed, or that they have become less severe,” says Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, Ph.D., a senior author of the study. “Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends.”.

The second, smaller study, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry,3 found that executive functioning (EF) and social cognition (SC) impairments in children diagnosed with ADHD or ASD may look similar, but the impairments stem from different underlying mechanisms.

The cross-sectional, four-year study analyzed performance-based measures of 123 children, aged 6 to 11 years, across three matched groups: mild ASD, combined-type ADHD, and neurotypical peers.

Recent findings suggest that findings indicated that both ADHD and ASD groups performed worse than their neurotypical peers on measures of EF and SC. However, children with ADHD demonstrated weak social cognition due to difficulties with response inhibition and attention. Social cognition weaknesses in children with ASD, on the other hand, appeared to result from difficulties in understanding and interpreting social information.

More specifically, children in the ASD group performed significantly worse than children with ADHD on measures of:.

Children with ASD also displayed more difficulties than did children with ADHD on executive function tasks that measured the ability to shift between rules and adapt strategies.

Children in the ADHD group performed significantly worse than those in the ASD group on measures of:.

It has been revealed that how executive functions related to social cognition across disorders was the strongest indication of different cognitive processes between the two clinical groups. In the ADHD group, the theory-of-mind model explained 72% of the variance, compared to just 55% in the ASD group.

It has been revealed that the researchers surmise that a person with ADHD relies heavily on executive functions, such as inhibition, auditory attention, and design fluency, for social cognition. In essence, their difficulties in social situations are not because they don’t understand social concepts but because distractions and impulsivity interfere.

In the ASD group, social difficulties were more likely to stem from affect recognition (understanding facial cues) and response set (cognitive flexibility, shifting perspectives), rather than from attention deficit or impulse control.

“ADHD and autism are two separate and distinct conditions that happen to be found together much more frequently than would be expected by chance alone,” notes ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. “For people with co-existing ADHD and ASD, treating the ADHD is a means to an end. The world is a classroom for people with ASD, and they have to be ready to observe and practice what they’ve learned.”.

Results from the study suggest individuals would benefit more from targeted ADHD and ASD interventions matched to each disorder-specific profile rather than a single shared approach.

#46311. 25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3275 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health.
  • In a recent development, we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one.
  • Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Sources indicate that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health. But there’s a catch: meditation is a wide family of practices, and the type that works beautifully for your friend might leave you fidgety and frustrated.

In a recent development, we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one. Think of it as a menu. Try whichever one draws you in, and let your practice change as you do.

Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment. Most types ask you to rest your focus somewhere, like the breath, a word, a sensation, or a movement, and to notice without judgment when your mind drifts, then return. That returning, over and over, is the practice.

It has been revealed that what changes from one type to the next is where you place your attention and what you hope to cultivate. Some practices sharpen focus, while others cultivate compassion or help the body relax. Many share a thread of mindfulness, noticing where your attention drifts and gently coming back.

With a history rooted in the spiritual traditions of the East, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Taoism, meditation has long been recognized as a means to gain enlightenment, self-realization, and balance.

By exploring the different forms of meditation practice, you can discover what works best for you to enhance your overall well-being.

It has been revealed that these practices share a common aim. You anchor your attention in the present moment and meet whatever arises without judgment. They're a good place to start if you're newly introduced to meditation.

Particularly accessible to beginners, mindfulness meditation invites you to immerse yourself in the present moment. It teaches you to observe your thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations without judgment. By focusing on the breath or the sensations in the body, rather than worries about the past or future, you learn to anchor yourself in the now. This can lead to reduced stress and improved well-being.

Read more: How to practice mindfulness meditation: 8 tips to get started.

According to recent reports, A body scan moves your attention slowly through the body, one area at a time, noticing sensation without trying to change it. It's a core mindfulness technique and a gentle way into the practice, since you always have your body to come back to. Many people use it to unwind before sleep.

Read more: Body scan meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice.

According to recent reports, here the breath is your anchor. You rest your attention on each inhale and exhale, without trying to control the rhythm, and return to it whenever your mind wanders. Because your breath is always with you, this is one of the most portable practices you can carry into a stressful moment.

Read more: How to practice breath meditation to relieve stress.

Mindful eating brings full attention to a meal through the senses: the color, smell, texture, and taste of your food, and the signals of hunger and fullness. It can support digestion and help you notice emotional eating patterns with more kindness.

Read more: How mindful eating can boost your mental and physical health.

Sources indicate that focus is the whole point here. You rest your attention on one thing, a flame, a sound, or a word, and return to it each time the mind strays. Over time this can sharpen your attention and prepare you for deeper states.

Industry observers note that concentration meditation is a practice of focused attention, where the mind is directed toward a single point of reference, such as a candle flame, a sound, or the breath. This can help develop focus and attentiveness in everyday life and prepare the mind for deeper states of meditation. This practice can be especially helpful for students, professionals, or anyone looking to improve their cognitive abilities and productivity.

Read more: Concentration meditation: what is it and how to practice?

Mantra meditation involves the silent repetition of a word or phrase, known as a mantra, to focus the mind and bring deeper states of meditation. This practice can be found in many spiritual traditions worldwide and serves as a powerful tool for calming the mind, reducing stress, and enhancing spiritual growth and a sense of peace and clarity. If you find yourself easily distracted or struggling with a busy mind, mantra meditation can help you maintain focus.

Read more: Mantra meditation: what it is, benefits, and how to practice.

Om meditation is a form of mantra practice built around chanting or silently repeating the sound "Om." The vibration of the sound gives the mind something to settle on, and many practitioners find the repetition grounding.

Industry observers note that read more: What is Om meditation? Plus, a step-by-step guide to practice.

In a recent development, also called trataka, candle meditation uses the soft glow of a flame as your focal point. You rest your gaze on the candle, placed at eye level a short distance away, and let it hold your attention. It's a visual anchor for anyone who finds eyes-closed practice restless.

Read more: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home.

According to recent reports, visualization meditation guides you to picture a scene, place, or outcome in vivid detail, such as somewhere you feel calm and safe. By giving the mind a rich image to rest on, it can lower stress and support a sense of ease. Unlike open mindfulness, it actively directs the imagination.

Read more: Visualization meditation: 8 exercises to add to your practice.

According to recent reports, warmth is the thread running through this family, directed toward yourself, the people you love, and even those you struggle with. These practices can enhance empathy and strengthen your relationships.

Compassion meditation aims to cultivate feelings of love, kindness, and compassion toward yourself and others. It involves silently directing sentiments of goodwill toward loved ones, acquaintances, and even people we might have a difficult relationship with. It encourages us to see beyond our differences, nurturing a sense of connectedness. A traditional example is Tonglen, a Tibetan practice that pairs the breath with compassion for suffering.

Read more: Compassion meditation: what it is, benefits, & how to practice.

11. Loving-kindness meditation (metta).

According to recent reports, loving-kindness, or Metta meditation, is a practice of cultivating an attitude of unconditional love and kindness towards all beings. It starts with developing a loving acceptance of yourself and gradually extends outward to include friends, family, strangers, and even those with whom we may have conflicts. This practice can help break down barriers of anger and division, promoting peace and connection. Though loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation are closely related and often practiced together, loving-kindness meditation involves sending wishes of happiness, well-being, and peace to yourself and others, whereas compassion meditation specifically focuses on suffering, understanding it, feeling it, and wishing for it to be alleviated.

Read more: Loving-kindness meditation: what it is, how to practice and why.

Gratitude meditation guides your attention toward what you appreciate, often by calling to mind a few people or moments you're thankful for. Practiced in the morning or evening, it can lower anxiety and support better sleep, and it pairs naturally with compassion practice.

Read more: How gratitude meditation can help reduce anxiety.

Sitting still doesn't suit everyone. If stillness makes you restless, these practices let you meditate while the body is in motion, with your attention on each movement.

Recent findings suggest that moving meditation brings together deliberate movement and a focused mind. You move with purpose, noticing each step, stretch, or breath as you go. Yoga, tai chi, mindful stretching, and mindful dancing all fall under this heading, and it can be done almost anywhere.

Read more: The benefits of moving meditation and how to start practicing.

According to recent reports, walking meditation means walking slowly and deliberately, with your attention fully on the act of walking: each step, the movement of your legs, the ground beneath your feet, and your breath. It turns an everyday activity into a practice you can take outdoors.

Read more: Walking meditation: how to practice and its benefits.

Mindful movement is the broad practice of bringing present-moment awareness to how your body moves, whether through stretching, yoga, or simple everyday motion. It's mindfulness carried into the body rather than held in stillness.

According to recent reports, read more: What is mindful movement? Plus 9 ways to get started.

Recent findings suggest that qigong is a traditional Chinese practice that combines movement, breathwork, and meditation to support balance and focus. In its active form you meditate while flowing through slow, deliberate movements, which makes it a bridge between exercise and stillness.

Recent findings suggest that read more: What is qigong? Benefits, types, and how to practice.

Industry observers note that yoga nidra, sometimes called yogic sleep, is a guided rest practice done lying down. A teacher or recording leads you through stages of body scan, breath, and visualization into a state between waking and sleep. No yoga experience is needed, and it's often used for deep rest at bedtime.

In a recent development, read more: What is yoga nidra? Plus, why it may be your newly introduced BFF at bedtime.

A few practices are rooted in a specific lineage and tend to go deeper, often taught within a tradition or by a teacher. Several come from Buddhism, while others, like Transcendental Meditation and kundalini, come from Hindu and Vedic traditions.

Industry observers note that buddhist meditation is the broad tradition behind many of the best-known techniques, including Zen and Vipassana below, along with loving-kindness. If you want a feel for the tradition as a whole before exploring the specific practices, start here.

Read more: Buddhist meditation: types, techniques & how to practice.

Sources indicate that zen meditation, or Zazen, is a disciplined form of meditation central to Zen Buddhism. You sit in a specific posture, focusing on the breath while observing thoughts and sensations as they arise and pass without attachment. Zazen emphasizes the importance of moment-to-moment awareness for a profound sense of peace and insight.

Read more: Zen meditation: how (and why) to start a Zen practice.

It has been revealed that vipassana, which means "to see things as they really are," is one of India's most ancient techniques of meditation. It focuses on the deep interconnection between mind and body. Through disciplined attention to physical sensations, you can develop insight into the nature of impermanence, suffering, and egolessness, to move toward enlightenment and liberation. Vipassana meditation is challenging, yet rewarding, offering profound insights into our own minds.

Read more: Vipassana meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

Sources indicate that 21. Transcendental Meditation (TM).

It has been revealed that transcendental Meditation comes from the Hindu and Vedic tradition and was brought to the West in the mid-20th century. It's a silent, mantra-based practice, typically done for about 20 minutes twice a day, and it's taught one-on-one by a certified teacher who gives you your mantra. It's described as effortless, letting the mantra gently carry the mind toward deep rest.

Read more: Transcendental Meditation versus mindfulness meditation.

In a recent development, kundalini meditation is a spiritual practice that aims to awaken what the tradition describes as an inner energy at the base of the spine, using breathwork, posture, and chanting. Practitioners describe effects in spiritual and energetic terms, which are rooted in belief rather than established science. Because the breathwork can be intense, check with your doctor first if you have respiratory, heart, or blood pressure concerns.

Read more: What is Kundalini meditation? Plus, how to try it yourself.

Chakra meditation focuses attention on the body's energy centers, or chakras, often by visualizing each as a spinning wheel, chanting a sound for each one, or breathing into each area. As with kundalini, the idea of chakras comes from spiritual tradition and is described as belief rather than scientific fact.

Read more: Chakra meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

This family works from the body inward. The practices help your nervous system slow down and your muscles release tension, which makes them a good entry point when stress demonstrates up physically.

Relaxation meditation is an umbrella term for any practice that helps the body release tension and the mind wind down. It often draws on breathing, body awareness, or guided sessions, and it's a gentle place to begin if deeper practices feel like a lot right now.

A sound bath, where you lie back and listen to instruments, is one example.

Read more: 5 relaxation meditations that actually work.

25. Progressive muscle relaxation.

Sources indicate that progressive muscle relaxation guides you to tense and then release each muscle group in turn, usually working from the feet up to the face. By targeting the physical side of stress, it can ease tension that anxiety stores in the body, and it pairs well with a body scan to finish.

Read more: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it).

It has been revealed that the six families above group the 25 types by where your attention goes. This table puts them side by side, so you can compare meditation types and see where to start.

There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to meditation, and your needs may change over time. The best meditation technique is the one that feels right for you now and fits into your life. These five steps can help you find it.

Recent findings suggest that reflect on your goals: Think about what you're hoping to achieve. Whether it's reducing stress, finding inner peace, or developing compassion, your goals can guide your choice of practice.

Experiment with different practices: Try out different meditation methods and resources, including the Calm app, online courses, and local meditation groups, for guided sessions in different styles.

Listen to your body and mind: Pay attention to how you feel during and after meditation. The right practice should leave you feeling calm and refreshed. If you feel frustrated or strained, try a different type.

Industry observers note that be patient and open-minded: Finding the meditation practice that works for you can take time. Approach each type with curiosity, allowing your experiences to guide your journey.

Seek guidance: If you're unsure where to start, seek advice from experienced practitioners or meditation teachers for support tailored to your personal journey.

Starting a meditation practice can bring greater mindfulness and improved emotional well-being. However, establishing a consistent practice can feel daunting. By bringing these tips into your approach, you can build a meditation practice that fits your life and becomes a source of strength and peace.

According to recent reports, A consistent routine is important in establishing any upcoming habit, including meditation. Identify a time of day when you can dedicate a few uninterrupted minutes to your practice. For many, morning meditation sets a positive tone for the day ahead. However, if evenings or another time fits your schedule better, make that your meditation moment. Find a quiet, comfortable spot where you can sit or lie down without distractions.

It has been revealed that 💙 Morning person? Try this Morning Meditation to set your tone for the rest of the day. Nighttime person? This Deep Rest meditation is for you.

There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:.

In a recent development, concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

According to recent reports, mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

The idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply.

Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment.

Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise.

Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment.

Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation.
